This provision shall not apply where a caster acts solely as an agent for another party who knowingly misrepresented the artifact's history, provided full disclosure was made prior to transaction completion. However, failure to disclose material facts regarding known provenance issues remains grounds for disciplinary action under existing regulations concerning honesty in trade practices.

The Desk encourages all market participants to exercise due diligence when acquiring magical items and report any suspected fraud immediately. Prompt reporting facilitates swift investigation and mitigation of potential harm to consumers and the integrity of the regulatory framework as a whole. Cooperation with authentication proceedings is mandatory upon reasonable notice.

Violations of this section may be prosecuted summarily without prior warning. Conviction carries automatic suspension pending completion of remedial training in ethical trading practices. Subsequent offenses will result in escalating penalties up to permanent revocation of all licenses and certificates held by the offender. The Guild maintains a zero-tolerance policy regarding deceptive provenance claims.

This section complements existing prohibitions on fraud and misrepresentation found elsewhere in these Accords, reflecting the unique risks posed by false attributions of magical significance. The Desk retains broad authority to interpret and enforce this provision as circumstances demand, within the limits set forth herein. All parties are expected to uphold the highest standards of honesty in all dealings involving licensed magical items.

body.heading: § 900.5 False Provenance of Relics and Related Deceptions — Continued — Continued
body.text:
The foregoing prohibition extends to any misrepresentation regarding the origin, age, or magical potency of an enchanted object intended for sale or barter. To assert that a mundane item bears ancient enchantments when it does not constitutes a material breach of trust and may be prosecuted as fraud under § 100.2(e). This includes fabricating pedigrees for artifacts, falsely claiming association with historic figures or events, and exaggerating the efficacy of protective wards or offensive charms.

Parties are encouraged to seek certified appraisals from registered Guild evaluators prior to major transactions involving relics suspected of containing active enchantments. Such evaluations shall be conducted in accordance with standards set forth by the Conservator's Office and may include non-invasive scanning techniques approved for public use. Refusal to permit such examination, where reasonable grounds exist to suspect falsification, shall be noted on the seller's license and may result in suspension pending further investigation under § 200.4(b).

The burden of proof rests upon any party alleging false provenance to establish by a preponderance of evidence that misrepresentations were made with intent to deceive. Witness testimony, documentary records, and technical analysis shall all be admissible as relevant evidence in determining the validity of such claims. In cases where deception causes tangible harm—including financial loss or physical injury—the aggrieved party may pursue civil remedies through standard judicial channels alongside any criminal penalties imposed by the Guild.

Repeated offenses regarding relic authenticity may lead to escalated sanctions, including permanent revocation of licensure and referral for trial under the Paradox Trial provisions of § 800 et seq. The Desk retains discretion to impose additional conditions on practitioners who have violated this section, such as mandatory ethics training or enhanced oversight during future transactions. All parties are urged to maintain scrupulous honesty regarding magical provenance to preserve the integrity of our shared professional community and protect the public from exploitation.

sections.title: Financial Fraud and Manipulation Generally
sections.brief: General prohibition. Cross-ref later 1001 sections.

body.heading: Financial Fraud and Manipulation Generally
body.text:
Any act of deception involving the deliberate manipulation of arcane, material, or ethereal assets to induce a party into an involuntary transaction or to misrepresent the nature of a magical contract shall be deemed a primary violation of the Autumnwood Accords. The Guild maintains that the integrity of the magical marketplace is the bedrock of civil stability within the Midlands; therefore, any mage or non-mage entity utilizing the arcane to distort the perception of value, ownership, or intent shall be subject to immediate investigation by the Aegis Magi. This prohibition encompasses, but is not limited to, the fabrication of magical provenance, the clandestine alteration of enchantment potency, and the use of coercive mental influence to bypass the voluntary nature of a trade. All such actions constitute a breach of the public trust and may result in the initiation of a Paradox Trial as outlined in § 800.2.

Furthermore, any individual found to be engaging in systematic financial fraud shall be barred from holding a Provisional Guild Pass, regardless of their political standing or historical contributions to the Innovators or Conservators. The Accords Desk reserves the right to seize all assets involved in a fraudulent transaction, including the forfeiture of the magical components used to facilitate the deceit. See § 1001.6 for specific rules regarding the transfer of assets and see § 1001.10 regarding the visibility of underlying obligations. Any entity found in violation of this section may be referred to the Archmage Sovereign for a determination of permanent expulsion from the Guild's jurisdiction.

body.heading: Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets
body.text:
The use of specific classes of magic within the context of trade, lending, or the valuation of assets is strictly prohibited to ensure the impartiality of the market. This includes, but is not limited to, spells of mass compulsion, truth-distortion, and any high-level divination used to extract private financial secrets from a counterparty without express, written consent. The Innovators may argue that such restrictions hamper the flow of information; however, the Conservators maintain that these spells undermine the fundamental principle of free will in commerce. Any mage utilizing these prohibited schools in a commercial setting shall face immediate sanction and potential sealing of their primary casting focus.

It is further mandated that the Quiet List shall remain strictly confidential. No mage shall recite, reference, or hint at the contents of the Quiet List in any tavern, marketplace, or public forum. Any attempt to use the existence of the Quiet List as a basis for market manipulation or as a tool of intimidation is a felony under the Accords. The Aegis Magi are authorized to use any means necessary to silence a mage who violates this confidentiality. For matters involving the specific reporting of forbidden research in trade, see § 400.1. For the consequences of unauthorized casting in public spaces, see § 500.2.

body.heading: Valuation After Alteration
body.text:
Any magical object or item that undergoes a significant transfiguration, enchantment, or physical alteration must be formally re-assayed by a Guild-certified appraiser before it may be traded or used as collateral. The mere act of alteration does not change the legal status of the item; for example, a petrified inventory remains a liability of the owner until the petrification is reversed and the item is re-certified. The burden of proof regarding the original state of the item lies with the seller. If a seller fails to provide a pre-alteration certificate, the item shall be valued at its lowest possible utility state for the purposes of all Guild-governed contracts.

In cases where an item is altered to increase its magical potency, the seller must disclose the source of the enhancement. If the enhancement involves the use of restricted materials or unauthorized schools of magic, the item is subject to immediate seizure by the Conservators. This rule ensures that the sudden influx of "enhanced" goods does not destabilize the local economy or introduce volatile elements into the Midlands. For inquiries regarding the custody of such specimens during the assay period, see § 400.4. For matters regarding the unauthorized growth of magical entities as a form of asset, see § 400.5.

body.heading: Illusion-Based Fraud
body.text:
The use of illusions to misrepresent the physical properties, quantity, price, or identity of goods, buyers, or sellers is strictly prohibited. A mage who casts an illusion to make a crate of common grain appear as enchanted wheat, or to make a small sum of gold appear as a mountain of wealth, is in direct violation of the Autumnwood Accords. This applies equally to the fabrication of a buyer’s identity; any mage who assumes the guise of a known entity to secure a favorable trade agreement shall be prosecuted for identity fraud. The Guild views the manipulation of perception as a direct assault on the sanctity of the agreement.

Furthermore, illusions used to obfuscate the true price of an item during a negotiation are considered a form of price-gouging and shall be met with heavy fines. If an illusion is used to hide a lien or a pre-existing debt on an object, the transaction is null and void, and the offending mage may be remanded to a pocket-prison. The Aegis Magi are tasked with patrolling major trade hubs to ensure that "visual honesty" is maintained. For procedures regarding the use of pocket dimensions as a means to hide these illusions, see § 400.2. For the reporting of material enchantments that may be mistaken for illusions, see § 900.2.

body.heading: Material Alteration of Traded Goods
body.text:
Any trade involving the aggregation, permissible transfiguration, or material alteration of goods must be accompanied by a full disclosure of the changes made to the base material. The burden of disclosure lies entirely with the seller. If a mage transfigures a common metal into a more valuable alloy, they must provide the chemical and arcane blueprints of the process to the Guild's records. Failure to disclose such alterations is a violation of the Accords and may result in the immediate revocation of the seller's trading license. This ensures that the "hidden" properties of a sold item do not cause unforeseen magical reactions for the buyer.

Historical annotations regarding the transmutation of materials are kept in the central archives; any mage performing these actions must cite the relevant precedents to ensure compliance with existing safety protocols. For example, the transmutation of lead into gold is subject to specific reporting thresholds as detailed in § 1001.8. Any transfiguration that results in a permanent change to the molecular structure of the trade good must be registered within three lunar cycles of the sale. For further details on the legality of transfiguring materials into laboratory equipment, see § 400.2. For the identification of fees associated with these registrations, see § 900.4.

body.heading: Endowments and Gifts of Magical Assets
body.text:
A magical asset provided as an endowment or a gift is not exempt from the laws of the Accords; rather, it is subject to specific oversight regarding its long-term obligations. A "hat that later bills the wearer" for its magical services is a classic example of a deceptive endowment. Any gift that carries a hidden cost, a retroactive debt, or a self-replicating fee structure must be disclosed in full at the moment of the gift's delivery. If a gift is found to contain a hidden "billing" enchantment or a parasitic mana-drain, the gift is declared a violation of the Accords and the provider shall be liable for triple damages.

Furthermore, the transfer of a magical asset as a gift does not transfer the liability of any existing liens or debts attached to that asset unless such a transfer is explicitly stated in a notarized deed. The Guild recognizes that many magical items possess "sentience-lite" properties that may attempt to claim ownership or demand payment; the owner of the original asset is responsible for suppressing such behaviors until a formal transfer of title is complete. For the identification of fees regarding these transfers, see § 900.4. For the reporting of material enchantments that might facilitate such "billing," see § 900.2.

body.heading: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
body.text:
All mages and merchants are required to provide a full and accurate disclosure of the composition, value, and inherent risk of any magical item offered for trade. This disclosure must be provided in a language that the buyer understands; a disclosure provided in a dead tongue or a complex arcane cipher that the buyer cannot read is not considered a "full" disclosure and is treated as a deliberate obfuscation. This includes the disclosure of any "side effects," such as minor telepathic echoes, unintended environmental shifts, or the risk of the item becoming volatile under specific conditions.

Failure to disclose a known risk—such as an item's tendency to teleport when exposed to moonlight—shall result in the immediate forfeiture of the sale and a permanent mark on the seller's Guild record. The seller is liable for any damages incurred by the buyer due to non-disclosure. The Accords Desk requires that all high-risk items be accompanied by a "Warning of Volatility" scroll. For the reporting of such material enchantments, see § 900.2. For the legal consequences of providing false provenance for such items, see § 900.5.

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
The transmutation of base metals, specifically the conversion of lead into gold, is subject to strict reporting thresholds to prevent the destabilization of the regional currency. Under the Autumnwood Accords, lead remains lead for tax and regulatory purposes until a formal assay by the Guild's Assay Desk confirms the permanence and purity of the transmutation. Any gold produced via transmutation must be declared to the Guild within twenty-four hours of the conversion. This ensures that the influx of "new" gold does not lead to hyper-inflation or the corruption of the market.

Mages who engage in large-scale transmutation for the purpose of flooding the market with gold are subject to heavy fines and may be required to contribute a portion of their yield to the Guild's treasury. The Innovators may argue that this stifles the progress of alchemical science, but the Conservators maintain that economic stability is a prerequisite for magical safety. For inquiries regarding the identification of fees for these assays, see § 900.4. For the reporting of these material enchantments, see § 900.2.

body.heading: Polymorph of Coinage
body.text:
The use of polymorph magic to alter the shape of coinage is strictly forbidden. The Guild maintains that the shape of a coin is not its denomination; a gold coin shaped like a dragon is still a gold coin, but a copper coin shaped like a gold coin is a criminal offense. Any attempt to use polymorph magic to deceive a merchant or a citizen regarding the denomination of a currency is a direct violation of the Accords. Such acts are considered a form of high-level fraud and will be met with immediate seizure of all the offender's current currency.

Furthermore, the use of polymorph magic to create "counterfeit" coins—those that possess the correct shape but lack the required magical signature of the Guild-approved mint—is a capital offense within the Guild's jurisdiction. The Aegis Magi are authorized to use "Truth-Sensing" wards in all major marketplaces to detect such discrepancies. For the reporting of these material enchantments, see § 900.2. For the identification of fees for legitimate minting, see § 900.4.

body.heading: Invisibility of Liens
body.text:
A lien is a legal claim on an asset; the fact that a lien is hidden from public view does not negate its existence. Furthermore, any attempt to use invisibility magic or "veiling" spells to hide a lien on a traded object is a violation of the Accords. An invisible lien is still a lien, and an attempt to conceal it is a deliberate act of fraud. All liens must be recorded in a visible, legible manner on the item's title or accompanying documentation. Any merchant who attempts to sell an item with a concealed lien shall be prosecuted for fraud.

If a lien is discovered to have been hidden using active magic, the offending mage shall be subject to the Paradox Trial as outlined in § 800.2. The Guild maintains that transparency in debt is essential for the health of the Midlands' economy. For the reporting of the enchantments used to veil such liens, see § 900.2. For the legal consequences of providing false provenance regarding an item's debt status, see § 900.5.

body.heading: Wish Used to Rewrite a Filed Return
body.text:
The use of a "Wish" or any high-level reality-warping spell to alter, erase, or rewrite a filed magical return or a notarized contract is strictly prohibited. A wish does not rewrite the stamp of the Accords Desk. Once a document has been filed and stamped by an authorized clerk, it is considered a permanent record of the Guild. Any attempt to use reality-warping magic to retroactively change the terms of a contract or the amount of a reported enchantment is a violation of the fundamental stability of the Accord.

Mages who attempt such actions are viewed as threats to the very fabric of the Guild's legal framework and will be subject to the most severe sanctions, including a permanent Seal of Silence or a Paradox Trial. The Guild's records are protected by high-level "Stasis Wards" to prevent such tampering. For the procedures regarding the Paradox Trial, see § 800.2. For the reporting of material enchantments that might be used to attempt such rewrites, see § 900.2.

body.heading: Wario Coin; Non-Recognition
body.text:
The Guild does not recognize the "Wario Coin" as a legal tender or a valid form of currency within the Midlands. The Wario Coin is classified as a private tender and carries no weight in Guild-governed transactions. Any merchant who accepts Wario Coins as payment for Guild-regulated goods or services is doing so at their own risk and is not entitled to Guild protection or mediation in the event of a dispute. Furthermore, the Guild will not facilitate the exchange of Wario Coins for any recognized currency.

Any attempt to force the Guild to recognize the Wario Coin as a standard currency is a violation of the Accords. The Aegis Magi are instructed to ignore any requests for currency conversion involving this token. For matters regarding the identification of fees for legitimate currency exchange, see § 900.4. For the reporting of material enchantments that might be used to fake Wario Coins, see § 900.2.

body.heading: Bag of Holding as Off-Books Vault
body.text:
Any storage vessel, including but not limited to a Bag of Holding, used to conceal assets from the Guild's oversight is considered an "off-books" vault. However, the Accords Desk maintains that "off-books" is still "books" if a clerk can smell it. The use of extra-dimensional storage to hide wealth from taxation, reporting, or seizure is a violation of the Guild's right to oversee the flow of magical assets. Any such vessel discovered in the possession of a Guild member that contains undeclared assets will be subject to immediate audit.

The Guild reserves the right to inspect any such storage vessels during a formal audit or if there is reasonable suspicion of fraud. The owner of the vessel must provide a full manifest of its contents. For the reporting of material enchantments that facilitate such storage, see § 900.2. For the identification of fees associated with the registration of large-scale storage vessels, see § 900.4.

body.heading: Secured Transactions in Bound Objects
body.text:
Any transaction involving a "bound object"—an item that possesses the ability to move, act, or defend itself independently—is subject to heightened scrutiny. Because such objects can "walk away" from their owners or act as autonomous agents, they are considered high-risk collateral. Any contract involving a bound object as collateral must include a "Binding Clause" that prevents the object from fleeing its owner or the lender during a dispute. Failure to secure a bound object properly during a transaction is the sole responsibility of the seller.

If a bound object leaves its owner's possession during a trade due to a lack of proper binding, the seller shall be held liable for the full value of the item. The Aegis Magi may be called upon to "tether" such objects during high-value negotiations. For the reporting of the enchantments used to bind such objects, see § 900.2. For the identification of fees for the notarization of binding clauses, see § 900.4.

body.heading: Layered Transfiguration Schemes
body.text:
Any series of transfigurations, enchantments, or physical alterations that are so complex that a reasonable toad would be confused are to be read as a single scheme. The Guild does not recognize "layered" deception where a mage uses multiple minor transfigurations to hide a major illegal one. If the cumulative effect of several minor magical changes is to obscure the true nature of an object, it shall be treated as a single act of fraud. This prevents mages from bypassing the laws of the Accords by breaking down a large violation into several smaller, "permissible" ones.

The Aegis Magi are instructed to look for the "intent of the weave" rather than the individual threads of the spell. If the ultimate result of a magical process is a violation of the Accords, the entire process is subject to sanction. For the reporting of complex material enchantments, see § 900.2. For the identification of fees for auditing complex magical schemes, see § 900.4.

sections.title: Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets
sections.brief: Named classes. Quiet List stays quiet.

body.heading: Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets
body.text:
Any mage, Innovator, or Conservator engaged in the facilitation of commerce, the brokering of arcane assets, or the management of guild-sanctioned vaults shall be strictly prohibited from employing specific classes of spells designed to bypass the cognitive faculties of a counterparty. Under the Autumnwood Accords, the use of high-level charms of compulsion, charms of suggestion, or any transmutation intended to alter the perceived weight or value of a physical asset during a transaction is strictly forbidden. Such actions constitute a primary violation of the Accords and shall be subject to immediate referral to the Aegis Magi for investigation. Furthermore, any spell that induces a state of "magical euphoria" or "docile compliance" in a potential buyer or seller is classified as a predatory arcane act.

The Guild maintains a strict prohibition on the use of "Veil-Shifting" and "Memory-Softening" magic within any marketplace, whether physical or ethereal. While the Innovators may argue for the utility of such magic in "market smoothing," the Conservators maintain that the sanctity of the buyer's will is the bedrock of the Midlands' economic stability. Any mage found utilizing these classes of magic in a financial context shall be subject to the Paradox Trial as outlined in § 800.2. The penalties for such violations may range from the permanent sealing of the offending mage's casting ability to a term of service in a pocket-prison, depending on the scale of the financial discrepancy caused.

Furthermore, no mage may use "True Sight" or "Identify" as a means of coercion to force a sale. While these spells are standard tools of the trade, their use to strip a seller of their "right to privacy regarding arcane secrets" is a violation of the Accords. The Guild recognizes the distinction between a professional assay and a predatory search. Any merchant who refuses to allow a standard, non-invasive assay by a licensed clerk may do so, but any mage who attempts to bypass this refusal using invasive scrying or piercing magic shall be fined. See § 1001.1 for the general definition of fraud.

The Quiet List shall remain strictly confidential and is not to be referenced in any public catalog, ledger, or marketplace declaration. No mage shall recite the names of items or methods contained within the Quiet List in any tavern, public square, or marketplace. Any breach of this secrecy by a mage, even if the breach is not intended for financial gain, shall be considered a felony under the Accords. The secrecy of the Quiet List is paramount to the safety of the Midlands; thus, any mage who discusses "Quiet items" in a commercial setting shall face immediate sanctions. See § 300.3 for the procedure of listing such items without public notice.

body.heading: Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets — Continued
body.text:
§ 1001.2 No Spell May Be Used to Manipulate Market Prices or Asset Values Directly. The use of arcane energies for the purpose of artificially inflating, deflating, or otherwise distorting the value of financial instruments is hereby prohibited. This includes spells designed to induce panic, greed, irrational exuberance, or despair among investors; to manipulate perceived supply and demand curves through magical means; or to directly alter the worth of currencies, commodities, or securities via enchantment. Such practices constitute a grave threat to the integrity of the global economy and are subject to severe penalties under this Code.

§ 1001.3 Exceptions for Legitimate Hedging and Risk Management Strategies Notwithstanding the foregoing prohibition, certain narrowly defined applications of magical theory may be permitted within regulated financial contexts, provided strict safeguards are observed. These include: (a) The deployment of protective wards or counter-curses by authorized risk officers to neutralize hostile magical interference in trading venues; (b) The use of divination techniques for market trend analysis, subject to prior approval by the Oversight Committee and full disclosure of methodology; (c) The employment of enchantments on physical infrastructure (e.g., server farms, data centers) solely to enhance resilience against natural disasters or sabotage attempts. Any such activities must be conducted in accordance with existing licensing requirements and monitored continuously by Guild auditors. Violations will result in immediate revocation of privileges and potential criminal prosecution.

§ 1001.4 Enforcement Powers and Penalties The Autumnwood Accords Desk is empowered to investigate suspected violations of this section, including but not limited to wiretapping communications, inspecting private records, and interviewing witnesses under oath. Upon probable cause being established, the Desk may issue an Emergency Preservation Order mandating cessation of all allegedly prohibited activities pending a full hearing before the Magistrates' Court. Failure to comply with such orders shall be deemed contempt punishable by fine or imprisonment at the discretion of the presiding judge. Convicted offenders face mandatory restitution payments calculated based on actual damages suffered by affected parties, plus punitive sanctions amounting to no less than three times their illicit gains. Repeat offenses will trigger automatic suspension from all licensed activities until further notice.

§ 1001.5 Definitions for Clarity In interpreting this section: "Market Prices" refers broadly to any quantifiable measure of value used in commerce, including stock indices, bond yields, exchange rates, commodity futures prices, and even intangible assets like brand reputation or user engagement metrics. "Direct Manipulation" encompasses both overt acts (e.g., casting a charm on a trader's brain) and subtle influences (e.g., embedding persuasive subliminal messages in advertising). The burden of proof rests firmly upon the accused party to demonstrate that their actions did not violate this prohibition, regardless of whether they intended harmful outcomes. This strict liability standard reflects the extreme gravity of undermining financial stability through supernatural means.

§ 1001.6 Relation to Other Statutes Nothing herein shall be construed to supersede applicable laws governing insider trading, market manipulation, securities fraud, or other forms of economic misconduct already addressed by civil and criminal codes. Rather, this provision serves as a complementary safeguard specifically tailored to address unique risks posed by magical intervention in financial systems. Where conflicts arise between provisions of this Code and external statutes, the more stringent standard shall prevail unless explicitly overridden by legislation enacted through proper channels. All regulated entities are reminded that adherence to both domestic regulations AND international treaties remains their paramount obligation at all times.

"See also § 1001.1 regarding general prohibitions on illicit spellcasting; § 600.4 concerning construct labor laws which similarly restrict exploitative practices."

body.heading: Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets — Continued — Continued
body.text:
The use of spells and magical techniques that directly manipulate financial instruments or market conditions is strictly prohibited within any jurisdiction subject to the Accords. This prohibition extends beyond obvious fraud or manipulation to include subtle forms of influence such as divination, charm, and compulsion aimed at swaying investor sentiment. The intent behind these restrictions is to maintain a level playing field for all participants in the financial sector and to prevent the exploitation of arcane advantages that could undermine market integrity.

Specifically forbidden are spells designed to predict future price movements with certainty, alter public perception of companies or assets, or directly affect the value of securities. Any casting of such prohibited arts within trading floors, exchanges, or related facilities shall be treated as a serious violation subject to immediate investigation and potential sanctions by the Aegis Magi. Penalties may include fines, suspension of licenses, and in severe cases revocation of operating privileges for institutions found guilty of facilitating illegal magical practices.

The burden of proof rests with the accuser to demonstrate that a prohibited spell was cast with intent to influence financial outcomes. However, any suspicious activity warranting further scrutiny shall be promptly reported to the appropriate authorities by responsible parties. Failure to report known violations may result in disciplinary action against negligent individuals or entities. The ultimate goal is to preserve fair and transparent markets free from the corrupting temptations of unchecked magical power.

This provision reflects a growing concern among regulators about the potential for arcane interference in economic systems, which could destabilize entire regions if left unaddressed. As magic becomes more integrated into daily life, the need for clear boundaries around its application in sensitive areas grows ever more critical. The Accords stand ready to evolve alongside technological and magical advancements to protect the public interest from emerging threats.

In sum, the prohibition of spells affecting financial markets underscores a fundamental principle: that power must always be exercised responsibly and within defined limits. Whether wielding swords or wands, all bearers of strength owe a duty to uphold justice and fairness in their dealings with others. By curbing misuse of magic in economic spheres, society safeguards its stability against forces far more unpredictable than any mere mortal could imagine. Let this law serve as both shield and sword against those who would exploit arcane talents for illicit gain at the expense of communal welfare.

body.heading: § 1001.2 Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets
body.text:
The use of forbidden magic within the sphere of financial transactions is strictly prohibited under this section, as such practices threaten both economic stability and public safety. Specifically, spells that manipulate perception, memory, or emotion are deemed unsuitable for commercial application due to their potential for abuse and long-term societal harm. Examples include charm person, mass suggestion, fear, and similar enchantments that may induce irrational decision-making among investors or consumers alike.

Furthermore, the employment of necromantic arts in banking operations is absolutely forbidden, given the inherent risks associated with summoning and binding spirits. The creation of undead servants for labor purposes falls outside acceptable bounds unless explicitly authorized by a special research permit issued by the Conservators. Any attempt to exploit such powers for profit without proper oversight constitutes a serious violation subject to severe penalties under the Accords.

In addition, the alteration of currency or trade goods via magical means is expressly banned, as it undermines the integrity of regional commerce and facilitates fraud on an unprecedented scale. Spells such as transmute metal to wood or alter self are particularly dangerous in this context, enabling the counterfeiting of precious metals or the degradation of valuable items without detection. Enforcement officers maintain vigilant surveillance over marketplaces to detect and punish offenders swiftly.

The Desk further mandates that all financial institutions employ licensed mages capable of identifying suspicious magical signatures indicative of illicit activity. Regular audits conducted by Guild investigators ensure compliance with these stringent regulations, with failure resulting in immediate revocation of operating licenses and potential criminal prosecution for responsible parties. Only through such rigorous controls can the Accords safeguard against the corrupting influence of black-market sorcery on the broader economy.

It is hereby declared that any individual caught utilizing prohibited spells for financial gain shall face summary expulsion from all Guild halls, forfeiture of accumulated credits, and mandatory sealing of their magical aptitudes by authorized Aegis Magi. Repeat offenders risk permanent banishment from the region and prosecution under existing criminal statutes. The collective well-being of society takes precedence over short-term profits derived from unethical practices.

This provision aligns with the overarching principles enshrined in §§ 1.7(c) and 900.2(a), emphasizing the importance of maintaining ethical standards across all facets of magical endeavor. By prohibiting dangerous applications in sensitive areas like finance, the Accords strive to preserve both individual autonomy and communal security for generations yet unborn. All members are urged to uphold these vital mandates with unwavering dedication and integrity.

body.heading: Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets — Continued — Administration
body.text:
The use of certain spells within the context of financial transactions and market manipulation is strictly prohibited under § 1001.2(a). Specifically, any spell that alters the perceived value or scarcity of an asset, regardless of its actual worth, constitutes a violation of these regulations. This includes but is not limited to illusions of abundance, glamours of quality, and enchantments that artificially inflate demand. Such practices undermine the integrity of fair trade and market stability.

Furthermore, any spell designed to influence the behavior or decision-making processes of potential buyers or sellers is forbidden under § 1001.2(b). This encompasses spells of compulsion, suggestion, intimidation, or seduction used solely for commercial gain. The intent behind these prohibitions is to prevent mages from exploiting their supernatural abilities to create an unfair advantage in financial dealings. All transactions must be conducted on a level playing field, free from magical manipulation.

In addition, the use of divination spells to gain insider information about pending market events is prohibited under § 1001.2(c). Mages may not utilize scrying, precognition, or other forms of foresight to anticipate price fluctuations, regulatory changes, or competitor actions for personal profit. Such practices distort the natural flow of commerce and enable unethical speculation based on privileged knowledge rather than sound economic analysis. The Accords aim to foster transparency and accountability in all financial activities involving magical entities.

Violations of these provisions shall be addressed in accordance with § 800 et seq., which outlines the penalties for breaches of the Autumnwood Accords. Depending on the severity and circumstances, offenders may face sanctions ranging from fines and license suspensions to permanent revocation of their right to practice magic within the Guild's jurisdiction. Repeat offenses will be met with increasingly stringent measures designed to protect the public interest and maintain trust in the financial systems regulated by the Accords.

It is imperative that all licensed mages familiarize themselves thoroughly with these restrictions and adhere strictly to them in their professional capacities. The integrity of our society depends upon the responsible use of magical powers, especially within sensitive domains like finance where even minor imbalances can have far-reaching consequences. By enforcing these guidelines consistently, the Guild safeguards both its members' livelihoods and the broader community from exploitation by unscrupulous practitioners seeking to bend reality for selfish ends.

see § 1001.2; see § 800.5; see § 300.1; under § 700.4. This clause serves as a critical safeguard against magical corruption of economic systems, ensuring fair competition and protecting consumers from predatory tactics that exploit supernatural abilities for illicit gain. The Guild remains committed to upholding these principles with unwavering resolve.

body.heading: § 1001.2 Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets - Administrative Oversight and E
body.text:
The administration and enforcement of the prohibitions outlined herein shall be vested exclusively in the Bureau of Economic Stability under the direct supervision of the Archmage Sovereign. The Bureau is authorized to conduct routine inspections of financial institutions, trading floors, and related facilities to verify compliance with these regulations. Inspectors shall have full access to all records, communications, and physical assets for examination purposes. Any entity found in violation shall face immediate suspension of operations pending a full investigation.

Upon discovery of prohibited spell usage or attempted usage within a regulated financial environment, the Bureau must initiate an ex parte seizure order pursuant to § 1001.4. This order authorizes the immediate confiscation of all materials and devices capable of facilitating such forbidden practices, along with any proceeds derived therefrom. Seized items shall be held in evidence until disposition by a competent tribunal. The burden of proving innocence rests solely upon the accused party, who must demonstrate beyond a reasonable doubt that no violation occurred.

Penalties for violations range from monetary fines to revocation of operating licenses and imprisonment. Fines are calculated based on the severity and duration of the offense, with maximum penalties capped at one hundred thousand gold pieces per incident. License suspensions shall be imposed for repeated or egregious infractions, lasting a minimum of six months. Criminal charges may also be pursued where appropriate under existing penal statutes. The Bureau is empowered to initiate proceedings directly without prior notice when immediate action is warranted to prevent further harm to public safety.

The provisions of this section are intended to preserve the integrity and stability of the financial markets against magical manipulation. Nothing herein shall be construed to limit the authority of regulatory bodies to enforce additional measures as necessary to maintain order and protect investors. The Archmage Sovereign retains discretion to amend these rules as circumstances dictate, provided such changes do not conflict with higher laws or established rights. All actions taken under this section shall be subject to judicial review upon timely petition by affected parties.

The Bureau maintains a detailed log of all inspections, seizures, penalties imposed, and related activities for transparency purposes. These records are available for public scrutiny unless classified as sensitive national security matters. Quarterly reports summarizing enforcement efforts shall be submitted to the General Assembly for consideration. The Archmage Sovereign may appoint special task forces with enhanced powers when required to address emerging threats or novel forms of prohibited conduct. Such delegations shall be temporary and subject to strict oversight mechanisms.

Ultimately, the goal of these regulations is to ensure that magic remains a force for good within society while preventing its misuse for illicit gain. Through diligent enforcement and fair application of penalties, the Bureau aims to safeguard both the economy and the public trust in financial institutions operating under its jurisdiction. Continued vigilance and adaptability are essential in an ever-changing landscape where new challenges may arise at any moment.

sections.title: Valuation After Alteration
sections.brief: Who assays. Petrified inventory is still inventory.

body.heading: Valuation After Alteration
body.text:
Any magical asset, artifact, or mundane item subjected to transfiguration, transmutation, or any other form of structural alteration by a licensed practitioner shall be subject to a mandatory re-valuation before it may be entered into the Guild’s ledger of commerce. The primary burden of initiating this assessment lies with the caster of the alteration; should the change be performed for a third party, the contracting party shall be held liable for the costs of the assay. The Accords Desk maintains that a change in physical state—be it the hardening of flesh into stone, the sharpening of iron into glass, or the expansion of volume—constitutes a fundamental shift in the object’s utility and marketability.

The official assay shall be conducted by a Guild-sanctioned Appraiser of the Fourth Circle or higher. No private valuation, regardless of the complexity of the arcane mathematics employed by the practitioner, shall be recognized by the Accords Desk as a final determination of value for the purposes of taxation or trade. This requirement applies to all items moving through the Midlands markets under the jurisdiction of Archmage Veyra. If a practitioner fails to submit an object for assay following a significant alteration, they shall be held in breach of the Accords, and any subsequent sale of said object may be voided by the Aegis Magi.

Furthermore, the Accords Desk explicitly clarifies that "Petrified Inventory is still Inventory." The transition of an object into a petrified, fossilized, or otherwise inert mineral state does not exempt the owner from their existing storage fees or their obligation to report the item’s existence. While the market value may be severely diminished by petrification, the legal status of the item as a piece of property remains unchanged. See § 1001.3 for further clarification on the persistence of property rights during state-change events.

body.heading: Illusion-Based Fraud
body.text:
The use of illusion magic to distort the perceived reality of a commercial transaction is strictly prohibited under the Autumnwood Accords. This prohibition encompasses, but is not limited to, the creation of an illusion of goods, the distortion of the perceived price, or the fabrication of a phantom buyer. Any practitioner who utilizes *Major Image*, *Hallucinatory Terrain*, or any derivative school of deceptive weaving to induce a sale is subject to immediate seizure of their arcane focus and a referral to the Paradox Trial for the determination of appropriate sanctions.

Specifically, the creation of "Ghost Stock"—where an item appears to be present in a warehouse or storefront but is actually absent—is classified as a high-tier offense of the Accords. Similarly, any attempt to manipulate the perceived scarcity of a resource via atmospheric illusions shall be met with heavy fines and a potential revocation of the practitioner's license to operate within the Midlands. The Accords Desk does not distinguish between "artistic" illusion and "commercial" illusion when the latter results in a transfer of currency or goods; if the buyer’s consent was predicated on a falsehood of the senses, the transaction is null.

The fabrication of a buyer is considered a felony of the highest order within the Guild’s jurisdiction. This includes the use of simulacra or illusions to create a false sense of demand, thereby inflating the value of the seller's goods or creating a fraudulent market history. Practitioners found guilty of such acts shall be barred from all Guild-sanctioned markets for a period of no less than ten years. See § 700.4 regarding the limitations of simulacrum testimony in these matters.

body.heading: Material Alteration of Traded Goods
body.text:
Any practitioner intending to sell a good that has undergone material alteration must provide a comprehensive disclosure of the changes made. This disclosure must be explicit and must be presented in a manner that ensures the buyer is fully aware of the item's history. The burden of proof rests entirely upon the seller to demonstrate that the transfiguration was performed within the safety margins established by the Conservators. If an object has been aggregated—such as the fusing of multiple smaller items into a single larger entity—this must be documented as a primary structural change.

Permissible transfiguration is defined as any change that does not fundamentally alter the "Soul-Signature" of the item, as defined by the Conservators. If a transfiguration results in a permanent change to the item's weight, durability, or magical conductivity, a formal disclosure must be filed with the Accords Desk. Failure to disclose such alterations constitutes a breach of the Goodstyle Artisan standards and may lead to a permanent ban from the Guild's trade circles.

Historical annotations regarding these regulations can be found in C.C.D. 6125, 7355, and 10155. These records detail the evolution of "Permissible Transfiguration" from the early days of the Accords to the current tensions between the Innovators and the Conservators. Practitioners are advised that the Aegis Magi may conduct random inspections of high-value inventory to ensure compliance with these disclosure requirements. See § 400.4 for related specimen custody rules.

body.heading: Endowments and Gifts of Magical Assets
body.text:
A magical asset provided as a gift or an endowment is subject to the same regulatory scrutiny as a standard sale, provided the asset possesses the capacity for autonomous action or delayed activation. Specifically, any item that "later bills the wearer" or imposes a recurring cost, fee, or obligation upon its owner after the initial transfer of possession shall be legally classified as an "Endowment of Magical Assets." This classification ensures that "gifts" cannot be used as a loophole to bypass the disclosure of hidden magical liens or recurring costs.

When an item is gifted, the donor must provide a "Certificate of Clean Title," certifying that no hidden geases, parasitic enchantments, or delayed-activation fees are attached to the object. If an item is discovered to have a hidden billing mechanism—such as a sentient hat that demands a monthly tribute of mana or gold—the original donor remains liable for the initial violation of the Accords. The recipient may seek a refund of the "gift" value, and the donor shall be subject to a fine for fraudulent endowment.

The Accords Desk recognizes that many magical items are inherently complex. However, the intent of the law is to prevent the "Trojan Horse" method of magical commerce. If an item possesses a "contractual" nature—where it performs a service in exchange for a resource—it must be declared as such at the moment of transfer. This prevents the circumvention of the § 600.3 prohibitions on unconscionable geases. See § 600.3 for details on geas as an unconscionable term.

body.heading: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
body.text:
All commercial interactions involving magical goods must be predicated upon full and accurate disclosure. The seller is required to provide a comprehensive breakdown of the object's composition, its current market value, and the inherent risks associated with its use. A critical component of this requirement is the language of disclosure; the Accords Desk rules that information provided in a language the buyer does not speak or understand is not considered "full." If a practitioner sells a volatile artifact to a layperson using only high-arcane cantrips for description, the practitioner is liable for any subsequent accidents or malfunctions.

The "Risk" component of the disclosure must include a warning of any known "volatile" traits, such as a tendency to teleport, a high chance of mana-drain, or a history of unpredictable behavior. For items of significant power, a "Safety Briefing" must be provided, and the buyer must sign a waiver acknowledging the risks. This is particularly important for goods sourced from the frontiers of the Midlands, where the stability of magic is less certain.

The Accords Desk maintains that transparency is the foundation of the Autumnwood Accords. By ensuring that buyers are fully informed, the Guild minimizes the frequency of disputes that lead to the Paradox Trial. Failure to provide a clear, linguistically accessible disclosure is grounds for immediate seizure of the goods and a penalty from the Aegis Magi. See § 800.1 for the range of sanctions available for such non-compliance.

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
The transmutation of base metals into precious metals is strictly regulated to prevent the destabilization of the regional economy. Under the Accords, lead remains lead for the purposes of taxation and trade reporting until such a time as the official Assay Desk agrees to certify the transmutation. A practitioner who creates gold through alchemy or spellcraft must submit their "Batch of Transmutation" to the Assay Desk for a formal verification of the metal's purity and origin.

Until the Assay Desk provides a "Certificate of Authenticity," any gold produced by a practitioner is considered "Uncertified Bullion" and may not be traded in public markets. Selling uncertified bullion as "Pure Gold" is a violation of the Accords and is punishable by a heavy fine and the temporary suspension of the practitioner's transmutation license. This rule exists to prevent the flooding of the market with magically-generated wealth, which would devalue the efforts of the Goodstyle Artisans and other legitimate producers.

The reporting threshold for transmutation is set at five ounces of precious metal. Any transmutation resulting in a yield below this amount is considered "Minor Transmutation" and does not require a formal Assay Desk filing, provided it is for personal use and not for resale. However, any sale of such "Minor" gold still requires a basic practitioner's license. See § 500.1 for rules on field casting for value.

body.heading: Polymorph of Coinage
body.text:
The physical shape of a currency unit does not determine its denomination. The Accords Desk explicitly forbids the use of *Polymorph* or any other shape-shifting magic to alter the appearance of coins, notes, or other tender. A coin that has been magically altered to resemble a larger denomination is considered a fraudulent counterfeit. This includes "Shape-Shifting Tender," where a coin may change its appearance depending on the light or the viewer's perspective.

The Guild's position is that the "Essence of Value" is tied to the magical signature and weight of the currency, not its visual representation. If a practitioner attempts to pass a copper coin that has been visually altered to look like a gold sovereign, they shall be prosecuted for fraud. This rule is designed to prevent the confusion of common merchants and to maintain the integrity of the Midlands' trade networks.

Furthermore, the use of polymorph magic on currency is seen as a frivolous waste of arcane energy and a direct insult to the stability sought by the Conservators. Practitioners found engaging in such activities may be ordered to undergo a period of "Arcane Probation," during which their ability to cast non-combat spells is restricted. See § 1001.1 for general financial fraud rules.

body.heading: Invisibility of Liens
body.text:
A hidden lien is still a lien. The Accords Desk establishes that any magical lien, debt, or claim placed upon a magical asset is legally binding, regardless of whether it is visually or magically concealed. An "Invisible Lien"—one that is hidden via *Invisibility*, *Masking*, or other concealment charms—is a direct violation of the Accords. All liens must be registered in a public ledger or at least disclosed to any potential buyer of the asset.

The purpose of this rule is to ensure that property rights are transparent. If a practitioner sells an item that is subject to a hidden lien, they are liable for the debt and any legal repercussions that arise from the debt's enforcement. The Aegis Magi are authorized to "Reveal All" on any high-value transaction, using detection spells to uncover any hidden magical signatures of ownership or debt.

A lien is defined as any magical binding that prevents the current holder of an item from fully utilizing its properties or selling it without the consent of a third party. If such a binding exists, it must be declared as a "Restrictive Covenant" in the sale contract. Failure to do so is considered a deliberate act of deception. See § 700.1 for evidence generally.

body.heading: Wish Used to Rewrite a Filed Return
body.text:
The use of a *Wish* or any other high-level reality-warping spell to rewrite, alter, or erase a filed tax return or a Guild registration is strictly prohibited. A *Wish* does not rewrite the stamp; the administrative record of the Accords Desk is considered a "Fixed Point of Bureaucracy." Any attempt to use reality-warping magic to retroactively change a past legal filing is a grave offense against the stability of the Guild's records.

The Accords Desk maintains that while magic can alter the world, it cannot overwrite the bureaucratic truth of the Guild. If a practitioner makes an error on a filed return, they must file an "Amendment of Record" through the standard channels. Attempting to "wish" the error out of existence is viewed as an act of magical insurrection and may be prosecuted as an attempt to subvert the sovereignty of Archmage Veyra.

Practitioners who attempt to use *Wish* for administrative purposes shall be subject to immediate impoundment of their magical focus. The Guild views the preservation of its records as a primary duty of the Conservators, and any magic that threatens the integrity of these records is treated with the utmost severity. See § 800.2 for Paradox Trial procedures.

body.heading: Wario Coin; Non-Recognition
body.text:
The "Wario Coin" is not recognized as legal tender by the Mages' Guild or any other authority within the Autumnwood Accords. It is classified as "Private Tender" and may only be used in transactions between private parties who explicitly agree to its acceptance. The Guild does not provide any guarantees for its value, and it cannot be used to pay Guild fees, taxes, or fines.

Furthermore, the Guild notes that the "Wario Coin" holds even less value than common copper in many regional markets. Practitioners are advised that attempting to use Wario Coins for the purchase of restricted research materials or the settlement of debts with the Aegis Magi will result in the transaction being rejected without prejudice. The Guild does not wish to be associated with the "Wario Method" of commerce.

While the Guild does not actively ban the possession of Wario Coins, it refuses to provide any protections for those who trade in them. If a merchant accepts a Wario Coin and later finds it to be worthless, the Guild will not intervene. See § 1001.1 for general financial fraud and manipulation.

body.heading: Bag of Holding as Off-Books Vault
body.text:
Any storage vessel that expands the internal volume of an object—specifically the "Bag of Holding" and its variants—cannot be used as an "Off-Books Vault" to circumvent storage fees. The Accords Desk maintains that "Off-books is still books if a clerk can smell it." If a practitioner stores items in a Bag of Holding within the Midlands, those items are still subject to the Guild's inventory taxes and safety regulations.

The reasoning is based on the "Presence of Utility." If a practitioner uses a Bag of Holding to store goods for the purpose of trade or long-term storage, those goods are considered to be "in residence" within the Guild's jurisdiction. The use of such bags to hide inventory from the tax assessors is a violation of the Accords and will be treated as tax evasion.

The Aegis Magi are authorized to use "Sense Volume" spells to detect the contents of such bags during routine inspections. If a practitioner is found to be hiding a significant amount of inventory in a Bag of Holding to avoid the "Storage Fee," they will be assessed the back taxes plus a penalty for "Bureaucratic Evasion." See § 900.3 for record retention.

body.heading: Secured Transactions in Bound Objects
body.text:
The Guild recognizes that many magical items are "Bound"—meaning they possess a degree of autonomy or are tied to a specific caster. Any transaction involving a bound object is considered a "Secured Transaction" and requires a "Release of Bond" certificate. Collateral that can walk away, fly away, or otherwise act independently of its owner's will is subject to special restrictions.

If an item is used as collateral for a loan and it possesses the ability to move independently, the lender must place a "Geas of Stasis" on the object until the debt is satisfied. Failure to do so, or the attempt to sell a bound object without the consent of its "Master" (if one exists), is a violation of the Accords. The Guild seeks to prevent the "losing" of collateral due to the item's own agency.

In cases where an object's autonomy is so great that it cannot be reliably bound, it must be sold with a "Warning of Independent Agency." The buyer must acknowledge that the item may act against their interests and that the Guild provides no recourse for such actions. See § 600.3 for geas as an unconscionable term.

body.heading: Layered Transfiguration Schemes
body.text:
When a practitioner performs a series of transfigurations on a single object—a "Layered Transfiguration Scheme"—the entire sequence shall be read as one single scheme for the purposes of appraisal and disclosure. If a sequence of changes is so complex that a "reasonable toad would be confused" by the final result compared to the original state, the practitioner must provide a full history of every step taken.

This prevents "incremental fraud," where a practitioner makes several small, seemingly insignificant changes to an object until it becomes something entirely different, thereby avoiding the reporting requirements of a major transfiguration. For the purposes of the Accords Desk, if the final product is unrecognizable from the original, it is a "Major Alteration" and requires a full Assay Desk certification.

The burden of disclosure is on the practitioner to provide a "Transmutation Map" for any item that has undergone more than three distinct material changes. This map must be filed with the Accords Desk before the item can be sold or traded. Failure to provide a clear map for a complex scheme will result in the item being seized for "Unregulated Alteration." See § 1001.3 for valuation after alteration.

sections.title: Illusion-Based Fraud
sections.brief: Illusion of goods, of price, of a buyer.

body.heading: Illusion-Based Fraud
body.text:
Illusion of goods, of price, of a buyer.

Any act of commerce involving the use of illusion magic to distort the perception of the tangible, the fiscal, or the corporeal nature of a transaction shall be deemed a primary violation of the Autumnwood Accords. The Accords Desk maintains that the integrity of the marketplace relies upon a shared reality; therefore, any mage who utilizes glamours to project the existence of inventory that does not exist in the physical plane, or to mask the physical decay of a product, shall be subject to immediate seizure of assets. This includes, but is not limited to, the projection of "phantom stock" to lure buyers into entering into binding contracts for goods that have been destroyed, sold elsewhere, or never produced. Such actions constitute a breach of the sanctity of the Midlands trade routes and shall be prosecuted under the standard of deceptive practice.

Furthermore, the manipulation of perceived price is strictly prohibited. A mage may not cast illusions that alter the visual representation of a price tag, the perceived quantity of a bulk shipment, or the perceived quality of a gemstone or reagent. The Guild recognizes that while the aesthetic appeal of a product may be enhanced through minor, non-persistent enchantments, any illusion that obscures the actual cost or the true weight of the item constitutes fraud. The burden of proof in such cases shall rest upon the seller to provide a "True-Sight" verification at the time of the transaction, ensuring that the buyer is interacting with the reality of the offer.

The most severe category of illusion-based fraud involves the fabrication of the buyer. The use of illusions to create a "simulated clientele" to inflate the perceived popularity of a shop, or the use of illusions to impersonate a high-status individual to secure favorable credit terms, is a felony under Guild law. Any mage found to have manufactured a "crowd" to create a false sense of demand shall be fined three times the projected value of the fraud. See § 1001.1. Any merchant caught employing such tactics shall have their trading license revoked by the Accords Desk. The Guild maintains that while the Innovators may seek to push the boundaries of sensory manipulation, the marketplace is a zone of absolute transparency. Any ambiguity created by magical means that leads to a financial loss for a non-caster shall be rectified by the Guild’s oversight committee, with the offending mage bearing all costs of restitution.

body.heading: § 1001.4 Illusion-Based Fraud
body.text:
The deliberate creation or manipulation of illusory phenomena for the purpose of deceiving another party constitutes fraud under these Accords, regardless of whether tangible property changes hands. This prohibition extends to all forms of visual, auditory, olfactory, tactile, and gustatory deception designed to induce reliance by a victim. See § 1001.2 Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets; § 700.2 Scrying of Closed Books.

Specifically prohibited are illusions that simulate the presence or absence of goods, services, or conditions material to a transaction. This includes but is not limited to: fabricating visual evidence of product quality; simulating verbal communications from non-existent parties; creating false sensory impressions to alter perception of value or risk; and generating deceptive environmental effects intended to influence decision-making. Under § 1001.3 Valuation After Alteration, any item or service subject to such deception shall be deemed materially altered for purposes of contract interpretation.

The burden of proving intentional misrepresentation rests with the accusing party, who must demonstrate that the illusory effect was purposefully employed to induce reliance. Mere accidental projection of false images or sounds does not trigger liability absent evidence of gross negligence. See § 700.1 Evidence Generally; § 300.2 Necromancy; Unsanctioned Arts.

Remedies for proven illusion-based fraud include rescission of the affected agreement, restitution of benefits conferred, and damages equal to the difference between actual value and perceived value at the time of reliance. In egregious cases involving systemic deception by a caster or organization, punitive sanctions may be imposed including permanent revocation of licensure and referral for criminal prosecution under applicable laws. Refer also to § 800.1 Discipline; Range of Sanctions; § 600.1 Contracts with Non-Casters.

The Desk maintains an ongoing interest in preventing the use of deceptive magical effects to undermine fair commerce practices. Parties are encouraged to report suspected violations promptly to facilitate timely investigation and remediation. Failure to disclose known illusory conditions may constitute waiver of subsequent claims for damages arising therefrom, pursuant to principles of good faith embodied throughout these Accords. See § 1001.1 Financial Fraud and Manipulation Generally; § 900.5 False Provenance of Relics.

This provision serves as a cornerstone of the Guild's commitment to maintaining integrity in all magical transactions and interactions. By prohibiting deceptive practices, the Accords seek to foster trust between parties and ensure that outcomes reflect true merit rather than manipulated perception. The spirit of this section demands vigilance against any form of magical fraud designed to exploit human vulnerability or gullibility for personal gain. Consult § 1.7 Construction; Aggregation of Conduct regarding cumulative violations.

[End of Page]

body.heading: Illusory Representations and Fraudulent Deception
body.text:
§ 1001.4 Illusion-Based Fraud
The intentional projection or manipulation of deceptive visual, auditory, or sensory phenomena for the purpose of inducing another party into entering a binding agreement constitutes illusion-based fraud under this section. Such conduct is deemed a substantive breach regardless of whether tangible property changes hands directly, as the illusory misrepresentation vitiates genuine consent and undermines the integrity of commercial exchanges governed by these Accords.

Specifically prohibited acts include but are not limited to: (a) casting glamours or similar spells upon merchandise to falsely enhance its appearance or value; (b) employing auditory illusions to simulate bidding wars or artificial demand; (c) fabricating illusory buyers, sellers, or witnesses to create false market conditions; and (d) using deceptive visual effects to conceal defects in goods. The mere capacity for such deception does not constitute a violation absent actual intent and execution designed to defraud.

Any party found guilty of committing illusion-based fraud shall face sanctions commensurate with the severity of the offense and resulting harm. Minor infractions may be addressed through remedial measures including restitution, fines, or mandatory education regarding ethical use of magical arts. More egregious violations warrant escalated penalties ranging from license suspension to permanent revocation coupled with exclusion from future Guild operations. In cases involving substantial financial loss or endangerment of public safety, the matter shall be referred for appropriate criminal prosecution alongside administrative sanctions.

Prevention and enforcement mechanisms include routine inspections of commercial establishments by authorized inspectors empowered to detect suspicious magical activity. Reporters of suspected fraud are encouraged to notify local Aegis Magi without fear of retaliation, receiving protection from retaliatory action in accordance with § 101.7. Repeated offenders may find themselves added to the Restricted List, barring them from entering certain zones or engaging in specified professions until further notice.

The Guild maintains that truthful representation forms the bedrock of honest commerce and public trust. Illusion-based fraud strikes at this foundation by substituting deception for reality itself. Consequently, such practices will not be tolerated under any circumstances as they erode confidence in legal transactions and expose all participants to exploitation. Strict adherence to this provision is essential for preserving fair markets and protecting consumers from predatory magical manipulation.

see § 1001.1 Financial Fraud Generally; see § 201.4 Misrepresentation of Skills; see § 300.5 Research Copies and Plagiarism; see § 900.6 Falsification of Records. This section shall take effect upon final promulgation by the Autumnwood Accords Desk.

body.heading: § 1001.4 Illusory Representations and Fraudulent Deception
body.text:
A representation made by means of an illusion, whether conjured in whole or part, shall constitute fraud if the maker intends to induce reliance thereon for pecuniary advantage. This includes, but is not limited to, the fabrication of a buyer's presence, the simulation of sufficient funds, or the creation of phantom inventory through optical or mental constructs. Any caster who knowingly employs such deceptions in the course of trade shall be deemed guilty of financial fraud under § 1001.4 and subject to penalties commensurate with the degree of deception and resulting loss.

The burden of proof rests upon the accuser to demonstrate that an illusory device was used with specific intent to mislead, rather than as a mere display of magical prowess. However, once such fact is established, any subsequent claim that the illusion did not materially affect the transaction shall be presumed false unless rebutted by clear and convincing evidence. This standard recognizes the inherent difficulty in discerning truth from artifice when one's senses are actively manipulated.

Casters who utilize illusions to bypass licensing requirements or evade regulatory oversight shall face additional charges for violating §§ 200.1 and 900.1 respectively. The Guild maintains zero tolerance for magical trickery intended to circumvent established controls, viewing such practices as a direct threat to the integrity of the entire system. Repeat offenders may be subject to permanent revocation of licensure and referral for Paradox Trial proceedings under § 800.2.

It is further provided that any damages arising from reliance on fraudulent illusions shall be recoverable as if the deception had been accomplished through conventional means. This includes, without limitation, losses incurred by victims who parted with property in good faith based on false representations induced magically. The courts retain broad discretion to award punitive measures designed to deter future misconduct and make whole those harmed by such treachery.

This section shall be construed liberally to encompass all forms of deceptive magical practice used for financial gain, whether performed directly or through proxies. Any evasion of this provision through technicalities shall not excuse liability but rather demonstrate a flagrant disregard for the spirit of the law. The Guild expects all licensed casters to uphold the highest standards of honesty and transparency in their dealings, refusing to exploit the vulnerabilities inherent in human perception for selfish ends. Violation of these principles strikes at the very foundation of trust upon which commerce depends, warranting swift and severe consequences.

The provisions herein shall take effect immediately upon filing and remain in full force unless expressly amended by subsequent rulemaking. All existing cases involving illusory fraud pending before any tribunal shall be adjudicated according to this section as if fully incorporated therein at the time of filing. This rule serves to close a critical loophole exploited by unscrupulous mages throughout history, ensuring that no further harm comes from those who would misuse their gifts for ill purposes. Let it be known that the Autumnwood Accords shall stand guard against such malfeasance, protecting both consumers and honest merchants alike from the wiles of deceitful casters. Any who oppose this mandate do so at their peril, for the Guild will pursue all violators relentlessly until justice is served in full measure.

body.heading: § 1001.4 Illusory Representations and Fraudulent Deception — Continued
body.text:
Whereas the provisions of this Part regulate substantive financial manipulations, § 1001.4 addresses deceptive practices involving illusory projections intended to mislead parties regarding material facts. This prohibition extends beyond mere falsehoods spoken with intent to deceive; it encompasses any deliberate creation of false sensory data designed to influence commercial judgment or contractual assent. The underlying principle is that no transaction shall be validated if its core premises rest upon knowingly fabricated perceptual inputs, whether generated by magical effects or technological means.

Specifically prohibited acts include conjuring phantasmal commodities to inflate apparent inventory levels, projecting artificial images of prospective buyers to simulate demand, and manipulating ambient conditions such as lighting, sound, or scent to alter a target's emotional state during negotiations. Such tactics are deemed inherently coercive, undermining the voluntary nature of exchanges governed by these Accords. Furthermore, any device constructed solely for generating deceptive illusions with commercial application falls under this section's purview, regardless of whether active projection occurs at the time of observation.

The burden of proof rests upon the accuser to demonstrate that the accused party knowingly employed illusory projections for fraudulent ends and that such usage materially affected the outcome in question. However, circumstantial evidence may suffice where direct testimony is unavailable; patterns of behavior consistent with deceptive practices may be admitted as corroboration. Notably, legitimate artistic or entertainment uses of illusion magic remain permissible so long as no commercial advantage is improperly derived therefrom.

Violations of § 1001.4 are subject to penalties commensurate with the severity and frequency of the offenses, ranging from monetary fines proportional to ill-gotten gains to permanent suspension of licensure for repeat offenders. In egregious cases involving substantial harm or repeated misconduct, revocation of all magical privileges may be imposed at the discretion of the Desk. Remedies available to aggrieved parties include rescission of tainted agreements, restitution of losses incurred, and injunctive relief to prevent further exploitation of deceptive techniques. The Guild reserves the right to pursue additional sanctions as warranted by the circumstances surrounding each violation.

This section stands in harmony with established precedents prohibiting fraudulent conduct under §§ 1001.1 through 1001.3, extending regulatory oversight into previously unpoliced domains where magical deception intersects with commercial activity. By establishing clear boundaries for acceptable use of illusory arts in financial contexts, the Accords seek to preserve integrity and trust within the broader marketplace while recognizing the unique capabilities afforded by advanced spellcraft. Compliance with these guidelines is mandatory for all licensed practitioners operating within the jurisdiction of the Autumnwood Hall.

body.heading: 1001.4 Illusory Representations and Fraudulent Deception — Continued
body.text:
Any representation or display that creates a false impression regarding the nature, quality, quantity, or authenticity of magical goods shall constitute fraud under § 1001.4(a). This includes but is not limited to illusions designed to conceal defects, exaggerate value, mislead purchasers about capabilities, or fabricate provenance entirely. The burden of proof rests upon the accuser to demonstrate that the deceptive act was intentional and material to the transaction.

Illusory Representations and Fraudulent Deception — Continued shall apply regardless of whether the deceiver possesses superior knowledge of the true state of affairs (§ 1001.4(b)). A caster may be held liable for knowingly permitting an illusion to mislead a counterparty, even if that caster did not personally create or direct the effect. This principle extends to clerks and agents who fail in their duty to verify representations made on behalf of the Guild.

Punishment for violation shall include disgorgement of ill-gotten gains, permanent revocation of licensure, and referral to the Paradox Trial for further sanctions (§ 1001.4(c)). In egregious cases where public trust has been severely compromised, a temporary ban on all commercial casting may be imposed until such time as the affected entity demonstrates full compliance with relevant statutes. Repeat offenders shall face additional penalties at the discretion of the Desk.

The provisions of § 1001.4 are not limited to direct transactions between individuals but also encompass indirect dealings where one party benefits from another's deception. For example, a merchant who knowingly sells defective enchanted items may be liable for damages suffered by end-users, even if no direct contractual relationship existed between the two parties (§ 1001.4(d)). Similarly, an employer who allows its agents to engage in fraudulent practices may be held vicariously responsible for resulting harms.

This section works in tandem with § 1001.5 regarding truthfulness in advertising and marketing materials. Any false claim or exaggeration made to promote magical goods shall be treated as a violation of both statutes simultaneously, subject to cumulative penalties where appropriate (§ 1001.4(e)). The Desk retains broad discretion to determine what constitutes an "illusory representation" based on the totality of circumstances presented in each case.

In all matters concerning fraud and deception involving magical commodities, the highest standards of honesty and integrity shall prevail. Those who seek to profit from misleading others will find themselves swiftly punished in accordance with these laws. The Guild stands ready to enforce these provisions rigorously to protect both consumers and honest businesses alike (§ 1001.4(f)).

sections.title: Material Alteration of Traded Goods
sections.brief: MATCH THE FILED PHOTO: aggregation; permissible transfiguration; disclosure; burden; cross-refs; historical annotations C.C.D. 6125 / 7355 / 10155.

body.heading: Material Alteration of Traded Goods
body.text:
Any merchant, artisan, or mage-trader engaged in the commerce of enchanted, mundane, or semi-sentient goods shall be held strictly liable for the material alteration of such items following the point of sale. Under the Autumnwood Accords, the integrity of a trade is predicated upon the physical and metaphysical state of the object at the moment of exchange.
