An "alteration" is defined as any change to the object’s primary form, weight, utility, or inherent magical properties that occurs without the express written consent of the purchaser. This includes, but is not limited to, the expansion of a container’s interior volume, the modification of a weapon’s reach, or the transmutation of a material’s base essence. See § 1001.3 regarding valuation after such alterations.

The burden of proof regarding the original state of a traded good rests upon the seller. If a dispute arises concerning the degradation or transformation of a product, the seller must provide a certified "State of Origin" manifest. In cases where the item is an enchanted artifact, the seller shall provide a recorded magical signature to accompany the physical description. If a buyer can demonstrate that an item has undergone an unauthorized aggregation—such as the merging of two distinct magical artifacts into a single, unstable composite—the seller shall be liable for the full restitution of the purchase price plus a punitive fee of twenty percent of the original value. Furthermore, any permissible transfiguration must be disclosed as a primary feature of the item; if a transfiguration is hidden or triggered by a mechanism not revealed at the time of sale, it shall be deemed a fraudulent alteration.

All transactions involving complex transfigurations must be cross-referenced with the established precedents for material stability. For instance, if an item undergoes a change that results in a net increase of mass or volume without a corresponding increase in utility, it shall be flagged for inspection by the Aegis Magi. Historical annotations regarding the stability of such items may be found in C.C.D. 6125, 7355, and 10155. Any seller found to have intentionally obscured the "Material Alteration" status of a good through layered enchantments shall face a Paradox Trial for deceptive practice. See § 800.2 for the procedure of such a trial.

body.heading: Endowments and Gifts of Magical Assets
body.text:
Any magical asset, artifact, or enchanted garment bestowed upon a recipient as a gift or endowment shall be subject to the Accords' regulations regarding "Deferred Consideration." A common point of litigation arises when a gift—such as a ceremonial hat, cloak, or staff—is found to possess a "billing" enchantment or a parasitic mana-drain mechanism that activates after a period of possession. For the purposes of the Autumnwood Accords, such an item is not a true gift but an unconscionable endowment. If a gift later bills the wearer, the recipient is entitled to a full dissolution of the debt and the immediate seizure of the item by the Guild’s enforcement agents.

The distinction between a "Gift" and an "Endowment" rests on the intent of the donor and the presence of a latent obligation. A gift is a complete transfer of ownership with no strings attached. An endowment is a transfer of use that carries a hidden, delayed, or recurring cost, whether that cost be in gold, mana, blood, or service. Mages who provide "free" magical items to the public or to fellow mages are cautioned that any latent mechanism designed to extract value from the user post-possession shall be treated as a violation of the Accords. Such items must be registered with the Accords Desk as "Conditional Endowments" before they may be distributed.

Furthermore, if an endowment is discovered to be predatory—meaning the cost of the "gift" exceeds the market value of the item by a factor of three or more—the donor shall be subject to a mandatory audit by the Conservators. Archmage Theron has decreed that the stability of the Midlands' economy relies on the clarity of these transfers. If a donor attempts to bypass these rules by claiming the billing mechanism is a "protective ward" or a "training exercise," the burden of proof remains on the donor to demonstrate that the cost is non-exploitative. See § 600.3 for related prohibitions on unconscionable terms in magical contracts.

body.heading: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
body.text:
The principle of Full and Accurate Disclosure is the cornerstone of all commercial arcane transactions. Every seller of magical goods is mandated to provide a comprehensive disclosure of an item’s composition, its appraised value, and its inherent risks. This disclosure must be presented in a manner that is accessible to the buyer. It is a specific violation of the Accords to provide a disclosure that is technically accurate but practically obscured. For example, providing a description of a volatile explosive in a language the buyer does not speak, or using overly dense arcane jargon to hide a catastrophic failure rate, shall be deemed a failure of disclosure.

Full disclosure requires three distinct components. First, the Composition: the seller must list all base materials and the primary schools of magic used in the item’s construction. Second, the Value: the seller must provide a fair market appraisal, adjusted for any unique magical properties. Third, the Risk: the seller must explicitly state the "Failure State" of the item—what happens when the magic fails, breaks, or is exhausted. If an item has a chance of teleporting the user to a pocket dimension, exploding, or causing permanent mana-burn, these risks must be highlighted in bold, legible script.

Failure to provide these disclosures shall result in the immediate voiding of the contract and a forfeiture of the seller's right to the purchase price. If a buyer suffers harm due to an undisclosed risk, the seller shall be liable for all damages, including medical costs and any necessary restoration of magical essence. The Accords Desk maintains that a buyer's ignorance, when facilitated by a seller's obfuscation, is a triable offense. See § 700.1 for the general rules of evidence in such disputes.

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
The transmutation of base metals into precious metals is a strictly regulated activity under the Autumnwood Accords. To prevent the destabilization of local economies and the flooding of markets with counterfeit bullion, the Accords establish a clear reporting threshold for all transmutation-based activities. Specifically, the transmutation of lead into gold (or any other base metal into a currency-standard metal) is not considered a "completed sale" for the purpose of tax and regulation until the item has been formally assayed by a Guild-approved assay desk.

Until such time as the assay desk agrees to the purity and permanence of the transmutation, the lead remains legally classified as lead. This means the seller cannot claim the tax benefits of gold production, nor can they claim the sale as a finalized transaction of high-value goods. This rule ensures that "temporary" transmutations—those that might revert to lead after a certain period or under specific conditions—do not bypass the Guild’s oversight. Sellers must present the item to a certified clerk who will verify the stability of the transmutation before it is entered into the ledger of commerce.

Any mage who attempts to sell gold produced by transmutation without first obtaining an assay certificate shall be charged with "Market Sabotage." This offense is treated with high severity by the Conservators, who view the unauthorized production of gold as a threat to the Midlands' prosperity. If an assay desk determines that a transmutation is unstable or "flickering," the resulting gold shall be struck from the records and the seller may be fined. See § 1001.3 for valuation after alteration.

body.heading: Polymorph of Coinage
body.text:
The Accords clearly distinguish between the physical shape of a currency and its actual denomination. A common form of fraud involves the use of polymorph magic to alter the appearance of a coin—making a copper piece appear as a gold sovereign or changing the size of a silver piece to mimic a larger denomination. Under the Accords, "Shape is not denomination." The magical appearance of a coin is irrelevant to its legal tender value; only the inherent magical signature and the weight of the base metal (as verified by the assay desk) determine its worth.

Mages who employ polymorph magic for the purpose of deceiving a merchant or a peer in a transaction shall be subject to immediate seizure of the fraudulent goods and a mandatory fine. This rule applies regardless of whether the polymorph effect is permanent or temporary. If a coin is enchanted to look like gold but remains copper in essence, it is a counterfeit. If a coin is enchanted to look like a sovereign but is actually a sovereign of lesser weight, it is a fraudulent alteration. The Accords Desk does not recognize "magical aesthetics" as a valid reason for a discrepancy in value.

Furthermore, any merchant who knowingly accepts polymorphed coinage without first performing a standard "Sense Magic" check shall forfeit their right to claim the currency as valid tender. This places a shared responsibility on the trade community to maintain the integrity of the local economy. The Aegis Magi are authorized to patrol markets and may confiscate any items suspected of being polymorphed for the purpose of fraud. See § 1001.4 regarding illusion-based fraud.

body.heading: Invisibility of Liens
body.text:
A lien is a legal claim on a property or asset as security for a debt. Under the Autumnwood Accords, the "Invisibility of Liens" principle dictates that a hidden lien is still a lien, and any attempt to render such a lien invisible or undetectable through magical means is a direct violation of the Guild’s transparency requirements. If a mage or merchant places a lien on a magical artifact, that lien must be recorded in a public registry or, at minimum, be detectable by a standard "Sense Lien" spell.

An invisible lien—one that has been magically masked so that it does not appear on a standard audit or cannot be detected by the owner of the asset—is considered a "Shadow Debt." The Accords Desk treats Shadow Debts as a form of predatory lending and a violation of the peace. If a buyer acquires an item with an invisible lien, they may petition the Accords Desk to have the lien made manifest. Once revealed, the lien must be satisfied before the item can be sold or transferred again. The presence of a lien, however visible, remains a valid encumbrance on the title of the good.

Any individual found to have intentionally hidden a lien to facilitate a sale is subject to a Paradox Trial for "Malicious Concealment." The Conservators emphasize that the clarity of ownership is essential for the stability of the Midlands. Mages who provide "clean" titles for items they know to be encumbered by hidden liens shall be held jointly liable for the debt. See § 700.1 for evidence generally.

body.heading: Wish Used to Rewrite a Filed Return
body.text:
The Accords Desk maintains a strict policy regarding the temporal and causal stability of financial records. It is explicitly stated that a "Wish" or any other high-level reality-warping spell used to rewrite a filed financial return is an illegal act of "Causal Fraud." While a Wish may indeed alter the reality of a past event, it does not—and shall not—rewrite the Guild’s official stamp or the chronological record of the filing. The act of filing a return is a bureaucratic fact that exists independently of the magical reality of the contents.

If a mage uses a Wish to "undo" a debt or "erase" a past expenditure, the Accords Desk will recognize the change in reality but will maintain the original record of the filing as a "Voided Entry." The mage will be required to pay a "Causal Correction Fee" to the Guild to account for the strain placed on the local reality. Attempting to use such magic to bypass the reporting requirements of § 900.1 is a severe offense, as it constitutes an attempt to manipulate the Guild’s oversight through unauthorized reality warping.

The Guild’s records are considered "Fixed Points" in the administrative sense. Even if a Wish makes it so that a debt was never incurred, the record of the debt's filing remains as evidence of the mage’s initial intent. Any attempt to use reality-warping magic to hide a history of magical misconduct or financial delinquency will be met with a Paradox Trial. The Accords Desk serves as the ultimate arbiter of what is "real" in the eyes of the law, regardless of what the current reality suggests.

body.heading: Wario Coin; Non-Recognition
body.text:
The Autumnwood Accords do not recognize the "Wario Coin" as a valid form of legal tender within the Midlands or any territory governed by the Accords. While these coins may circulate in private markets or as tokens of personal favor, they hold no value in the eyes of the Guild, the Conservators, or the Innovators. They are classified as "Private Tender" and are not to be accepted as payment for any goods, services, or fees required by the Accords Desk.

Mages or merchants who attempt to demand Wario Coins as payment for Guild-regulated services shall be denied the transaction, and the merchant may be fined for attempting to substitute unauthorized currency. Furthermore, the Wario Coin is not recognized as a valid collateral for secured transactions. If a merchant attempts to use Wario Coins to settle a debt with a Guild-affiliated entity, the debt shall remain outstanding until paid in approved currency (gold, silver, or authorized mana-credits).

The Guild’s refusal to recognize Wario Coins is absolute. No amount of "Waluigi-based" advocacy or "Wario-centric" commerce can alter this status. The Accords Desk advises all travelers to ensure their purses are filled with recognized tender before attempting to conduct business in the Autumn Wood. See § 900.4 for identify fees.

body.heading: Bag of Holding as Off-Books Vault
body.text:
The use of a "Bag of Holding" or any similar extradimensional storage vessel as an "off-books" vault is strictly prohibited. The Accords Desk holds that "off-books" is a status of accounting, not a physical location. If a clerk can smell the magic, the contents are considered part of the official ledger. Any storage vessel that creates a pocket dimension or a separate spatial plane for the purpose of concealing assets from the Guild’s audit is a violation of § 900.3.

Mages who utilize extradimensional storage to hide contraband, unauthorized research materials, or unregistered wealth are liable for "Constructive Possession." This means that even if the item is not physically present in the Midlands, its presence in a portable extradimensional space accessible by the owner constitutes possession within the jurisdiction of the Accords. During an audit, any such storage vessel found in a mage's possession must be opened and its contents cataloged.

Failure to report the existence of a Bag of Holding or similar vessel as a "Storage Asset" during the initial registration of a mage's workshop is a violation of the Duty to File. The Guild maintains that the ability to hide assets in another dimension does not grant a right to secrecy from the Sovereign. If a bag is found to contain "off-books" items, the owner shall be subject to a fine of five percent of the total value of the concealed goods. See § 900.2 regarding reporting of material enchantments.

body.heading: Secured Transactions in Bound Objects
body.text:
A "Bound Object" is defined as any item—be it a book, a sword, a piece of jewelry, or a sentient construct—that possesses the capacity for independent movement or autonomous action. The Accords Desk warns that these items are "Collateral that can walk away." Any transaction involving a Bound Object as collateral for a loan or a contract must include a "Binding Tether" or a "Geas of Immobilization" to ensure the collateral remains stationary and accessible to the creditor.

If a Bound Object moves from its agreed-upon location without the owner’s express command, it is considered a "Breach of Security." The lender is entitled to immediate repossession of the object, and the borrower may be charged with "Collateral Flight." To prevent such incidents, the Accords Desk recommends the use of a "Stasis Ward" during the period the object is held as security. Any contract that does not explicitly mention the containment of autonomous movement is considered poorly drafted and may be voided in favor of the creditor.

Furthermore, if a Bound Object is used as collateral and it acts with "Malice" against the creditor, the borrower shall be held strictly liable for all damages caused by the object. The owner of a Bound Object is responsible for its actions at all times, whether it is currently being held as collateral or is in their own possession. See § 600.2 regarding Familiars as Agents.

body.heading: Layered Transfiguration Schemes
body.text:
When determining the legality of a transfiguration, the Accords Desk shall apply the "Reasonable Toad" standard. If a transfiguration scheme is so complex, layered, or multi-staged that a "reasonable toad" (defined as a standard, non-sentient amphibian with average cognitive faculties) would be confused as to the item's primary purpose or current state, the entire scheme shall be read as a single, unified transaction. This prevents mages from bypassing "Material Alteration" laws by breaking a single change into multiple, seemingly minor steps.

For example, if a merchant transfigures a chair into a table, then the table into a stool, then the stool into a chair of a different color, the Accords Desk will not view these as three separate events. Instead, they will be viewed as a single "Layered Transfiguration Scheme" designed to obfuscate the final outcome. If the final result differs significantly from the original item without a corresponding disclosure, the seller shall be held liable for the entire sequence of alterations.

Any merchant who utilizes "Nested Transfigurations"—where one change is hidden inside another—must provide a "Full Schematic" of the item's potential states at the time of sale. If the schematic is missing or if the item undergoes a state change that was not listed in the schematic, the transaction is deemed fraudulent. The goal of this rule is to ensure that the consumer is not surprised by a "cascade" of magical effects that occur over time or through repeated interaction. See § 1001.5 regarding Material Alteration.

sections.title: Endowments and Gifts of Magical Assets
sections.brief: A hat that later bills the wearer is an endowment. Catchline from the photo.

body.heading: Endowments and Gifts of Magical Assets
body.text:
Any magical asset, artifact, or enchanted implement bestowed upon a recipient by a member of the Mages' Guild, or any licensed practitioner thereof, shall be legally classified as an endowment. This classification applies regardless of whether the transfer of the asset was intended as a gift, a loan, a reward for service, or a component of a larger commercial transaction. The primary distinction of an endowment, as established by the Autumnwood Accords, is the inherent potential for the asset to exert ongoing influence, provide persistent utility, or incur recurring obligations upon the holder. For the purposes of these regulations, a hat that later bills the wearer is an endowment. This specific precedent ensures that the mere act of "gifting" an item does not exempt the donor from the reporting requirements of § 900.2, nor does it shield the donor from liability should the asset possess latent properties that violate the Accord's safety standards.

Furthermore, any asset provided as an endowment must be registered with the nearest Guild clerk to ensure that any "hidden" costs—be they mana-taxation, psychic feedback, or material degradation—are disclosed to the recipient. Failure to register an endowment can result in the immediate seizure of the asset by the Aegis Magi, as the Guild maintains that any unmonitored magical gift is a potential vector for unauthorized influence. See § 1001.15 regarding the layering of such gifts. If a recipient discovers that a gifted item is subject to a "billing" mechanism not disclosed at the time of bestowal, the donor shall be held liable for triple the value of the first three cycles of the billing, plus any punitive fees mandated by the Archmage Sovereign's current decree.

body.heading: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
body.text:
All magical items, reagents, and enchanted services offered for trade or sale within the jurisdiction of the Autumnwood Accords must be accompanied by full and accurate disclosure. This disclosure must encompass the item’s magical composition, its appraised market value, and any inherent risks associated with its use. The Guild maintains a strict standard of transparency: a disclosure that is true in a language the buyer does not speak is not full. Therefore, if a merchant utilizes a linguistic charm or a complex arcane dialect to describe the properties of a cursed blade or a volatile potion, the transaction shall be deemed fraudulent. The seller must provide a translation in the common tongue of the region or a dialect clearly understood by the purchaser.

Risk disclosure must be specific. A merchant cannot simply state that an item is "powerful" without detailing the specific magnitude of its magical output and the potential for catastrophic failure, such as localized rift generation or unintended transmutation. If an item possesses a "sentience threshold" or a "personality drift," these must be listed as primary hazards. Failure to provide such disclosures shall result in the immediate voiding of the sale and a mandatory referral to the Paradox Trial for the offending merchant. See § 700.1 for evidence regarding the intent of the seller. The Guild shall not recognize "buyer beware" as a valid defense against the sale of undisclosed hazardous enchantments.

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
The transmutation of base metals into precious metals remains a primary area of fiscal oversight within the Guild. Pursuant to the Accords, the transmutation of lead into gold, or any other noble metal, does not constitute a change in the asset’s taxable status until a formal assay has been performed and approved by the Guild's designated assay desk. For the purposes of immediate reporting, lead remains lead for tax until the assay desk agrees otherwise. This rule prevents the rapid cycling of assets to evade the reporting fees mandated in § 900.4. Any mage attempting to sell "newly minted" gold without a corresponding transmutation certificate from the assay desk shall have the gold confiscated as contraband.

The assay desk is the sole authority capable of certifying the purity and "magical lineage" of transmuted gold. If the transmutation process involved forbidden schools of magic—as defined by Archmage Theron’s Conservator mandates—the resulting gold is subject to immediate seizure and the mage shall be remanded for a Paradox Trial. No merchant may claim a tax credit for "material improvement" until the Guild has verified that the gold was not produced via unauthorized blood tithes or other illicit arcane methods. See § 1001.3 for valuation after alteration.

body.heading: Polymorph of Coinage
body.text:
The Guild strictly prohibits the use of polymorphancy or any other shape-shifting enchantment to alter the physical appearance of currency for the purpose of deception. It is a fundamental principle of the Accords that shape is not denomination. A gold coin that has been magically reshaped into a silver coin, or a copper piece enlarged to the size of a dinner plate, retains its original denomination. Any attempt to pass a polymorphed coin as a different denomination constitutes a Grade-A financial fraud and is punishable by the immediate sealing of the perpetrator's magic.

Furthermore, the Guild does not recognize any currency that has been altered to mimic the aesthetic of restricted currencies, such as those of the Regal Empire or the Iron Legion. If a mage creates a "custom" coin that bears a resemblance to an enemy's tender, the coin is considered a counterfeit and the creator is liable for treasonous conduct against the Accords. Mages are encouraged to use standard Guild-approved tokens for internal transactions to avoid the complications of shape-shifting. See § 1001.4 for illusion-based fraud.

body.heading: Invisibility of Liens
body.text:
The Guild recognizes that magical liens—debts secured by an enchanted object—may be hidden through various means, including concealment charms or spatial folding. However, the Accords state clearly that a hidden lien is still a lien. Any agreement wherein a magical asset is pledged as collateral must be recorded in a public ledger or a shared vault accessible by the Guild's auditors. An invisible one is a violation of the transparency statutes. If a mage attempts to sell an item that is secretly encumbered by a lien, the transaction is void, and the mage may face fines for "Arcane Obfuscation."

In cases where a lien is rendered invisible via a high-level concealment spell, the Guild reserves the right to "force-reveal" the debt. If a lien is found to be hidden from the buyer, the seller is liable for the full extent of the debt plus a penalty of 50% of the item's current value. This ensures that the flow of magical goods remains unencumbered by clandestine debts that could destabilize the local economy. For disputes regarding the visibility of magical contracts, see § 600.3.

body.heading: Wish Used to Rewrite a Filed Return
body.text:
The Guild maintains a strict distinction between the manipulation of reality and the manipulation of administrative records. While a "Wish" or a similar high-level reality-warping spell may be used to alter the physical state of the world, it has no standing in the administrative courts of the Mages' Guild. Specifically, a wish does not rewrite the stamp. If a mage has filed a formal magical return or a report of a material enchantment, that record is considered a fixed point in the Guild’s bureaucratic timeline. Any attempt to use a reality-warping spell to "un-happen" a filing or to change the contents of a previously submitted document is considered an act of administrative sabotage.

Mages who attempt to use reality-warping to circumvent the reporting requirements of § 900.1 shall be subject to immediate detention. The Guild’s records are protected by a "Temporal Anchor" and "Static Seal," ensuring that even the most powerful desires cannot erase the fact of a filing. If a mage wishes to correct an error in a filed return, they must follow the standard amendment procedure rather than attempting to rewrite the history of the filing. See § 900.3 for record retention policies.

body.heading: Wario Coin; Non-Recognition
body.text:
The Mages' Guild officially declares that the "Wario Coin" is not recognized as a legal tender within the Midlands or any territory governed by the Autumnwood Accords. It is classified strictly as private tender. Because it lacks a standardized mana-back and is not issued by a recognized sovereign or the Guild itself, it holds no value in official transactions. Furthermore, "points" associated with its use are even less so, and the Guild will not accept them as consideration for any services, fees, or permits.

Mages who attempt to use Wario Coins to settle debts with the Guild or to purchase restricted research materials will find their transactions rejected without prejudice. The Guild will not convert Wario Coins into Guild tender, nor will it provide any exchange services for them. The only interaction the Guild shall have with Wario Coins is to refuse them as payment. See § 1001.1 for financial fraud and manipulation generally.

body.heading: Bag of Holding as Off-Books Vault
body.text:
Any spatial storage device, including but not limited to the "Bag of Holding," "Portable Hole," or "Pocket Dimension," is subject to the Guild's oversight regarding the storage of illicit goods. The Accords state that off-books is still books if a clerk can smell it. This means that while a mage may not be required to list every minor personal item stored in a spatial fold, any items of significant magical power, prohibited reagents, or stolen artifacts must be declared. The "scent" of an item refers to its magical signature, which remains detectable to trained Guild auditors regardless of the spatial displacement.

Mages who use spatial storage to hide "off-books" assets from the tax collectors of the Guild are in violation of § 900.2. If a bag or pocket dimension is found to contain undeclared material enchantments or prohibited schools of magic, the owner is liable for the full weight of the non-disclosure penalties. The Guild reserves the right to "audit" any spatial storage device during a standard inspection. See § 900.4 for identify fees.

body.heading: Secured Transactions in Bound Objects
body.text:
The Guild recognizes that certain magical objects, such as sentient artifacts, familiars, or bound constructs, possess the capacity for autonomous movement. Transactions involving such items are classified as "Secured Transactions in Bound Objects." Because collateral that can walk away presents a significant risk to the integrity of the marketplace, any such item pledged as collateral must be placed under a "Stasis Ward" or a "Geas of Compliance" during the duration of the loan.

A lender is not entitled to the full use of a bound object as collateral; they are only entitled to the value of the object. If a sentient artifact "flees" its lender or a bound construct "walks away" from a secured transaction, the lender must report the escape immediately to the Aegis Magi. Failure to report an escaped piece of collateral may result in the lender being held liable for the full value of the debt as if the item were still in their possession. See § 600.2 for familiars as agents.

body.heading: Layered Transfiguration Schemes
body.text:
When a mage attempts to perform a series of transfigurations on a single object to hide its true nature or to bypass specific regulations, these actions shall be viewed as a single, continuous act. The Guild maintains that a layered transfiguration scheme is read as one scheme if a reasonable toad would be confused. This "Toad Standard" is used to prevent mages from performing minor, seemingly innocent transmutations to circumvent the restrictions on more significant, prohibited changes.

If a merchant sells a "wooden chair" that has been transfigured three times—first from a tree, then into a chair, then into a "chair of many faces"—the Guild will treat the final sale as a sale of a "Chair of Many Faces." The seller cannot claim that the initial transfigurations were separate, legal acts. If the final result of the layered scheme violates any safety standards or is a prohibited school of magic, the entire chain of transmutations is deemed illegal. See § 1001.5 for material alteration of traded goods.

sections.title: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
sections.brief: Full and accurate. True in a language the buyer does not speak is not full.

body.heading: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
body.text:
Under the authority of the Autumnwood Accords and the regulatory oversight of the Mages' Guild, all commercial transactions involving enchanted,Thaumaturgic, or magically-augmented commodities shall be governed by the principle of Absolute Transparency. It is the decree of Archmage Veyra that the asymmetry of magical knowledge shall not be exploited for the purpose of illicit profit or the endangerment of the uninitiated. Any mage, artisan, or merchant engaged in the sale, trade, or transfer of magical assets—whether such assets be wands, scrolls, sentient constructs, or enchanted reagents—is strictly mandated to provide a full and accurate disclosure of the item’s composition, its current market value, and its inherent risks. Failure to provide such disclosures shall constitute a breach of the Accords and may result in immediate referral to the Aegis Magi for investigation, as well as potential referral to the Paradox Trial for the adjudication of magical fraud.

The requirement of "full and accurate" disclosure is interpreted by the Guild as a comprehensive accounting of the item’s metaphysical properties. This includes, but is not limited to, the potency of the primary enchantment, the duration of the effect, the source of the mana used in its creation, and any known volatile side effects. A seller may not omit a known risk simply because it is deemed "statistically improbable" or "minor" in the eyes of a practitioner. For example, if a protective ward possesses a non-zero chance of causing localized gravity inversion upon expiration, such a risk must be explicitly stated. Furthermore, the composition of the item must be disclosed in its entirety; an enchanted blade forged from iron infused with shadow-essence must be identified as such, rather than being sold merely as a "darkened steel blade." Any obfuscation of materials intended to hide the provenance of forbidden components shall be treated as a high-tier violation of the Accords.

The Guild further establishes that truth in a language the buyer does not speak is not considered "full" disclosure. This provision is designed to prevent the sale of dangerous artifacts to laypeople or foreign nationals who lack the linguistic capacity to comprehend the warnings provided. If a transaction occurs between a Guild-certified practitioner and a non-practitioner, or between two parties of different linguistic backgrounds, the disclosure must be rendered in a common tongue understood by the recipient. The seller bears the entire burden of ensuring that the buyer comprehends the specific dangers, limitations, and costs associated with the acquisition. Providing a list of warnings in a dead tongue or a complex arcane dialect to a common laborer does not satisfy the requirements of § 1001.7. In such instances, the seller shall be held liable for any subsequent damages, regardless of whether the information provided was technically "accurate" in its original form.

Regarding the valuation of magical assets, all parties must agree upon a fair market price that reflects the current state of the item. Any alteration to the item’s potency or composition—whether through wear, magical decay, or intentional modification—must be reflected in the final valuation. See § 1001.3 for specific protocols regarding valuation after alteration. A seller who knowingly overvalues an item by concealing its degradation or under-enchanted state shall be subject to the penalties outlined in § 1001.1. Furthermore, the Guild notes that while the Wario Coin is not recognized as a legal tender of the Guild, any trade involving private currency or barter must still adhere to the disclosure requirements of this section. All transactions involving the sale of items with "Restricted Research" status must also be accompanied by a certificate of permission from the Innovators, as overseen by Janna Brightspark, to ensure that the transfer of such items does not violate the broader safety mandates of the Autumnwood Accords.

body.heading: § 1001.7 Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
body.text: Whereas magic items often possess intricate enchantments or hidden flaws that may not be immediately apparent to the untrained eye, it is hereby deemed unconscionable for any seller to conceal material defects, superior qualities, or potential dangers inherent in the goods offered for sale. To this end, every vendor of magical artifacts must provide full and truthful disclosure of an item's composition, current value, and associated risks prior to finalizing a transaction. This obligation extends beyond mere verbal description and requires written certification by a qualified appraiser when the item exceeds a certain monetary threshold or possesses unique properties that could impact its safe usage. Failure to comply with these disclosure mandates shall constitute grounds for contract rescission and may subject the offending party to punitive damages equal to twice the purchase price, plus all reasonable costs incurred in mitigating any harm resulting from reliance on inaccurate representations. Furthermore, buyers are expressly warned that they bear sole responsibility for verifying the authenticity and condition of any magical goods procured outside official channels, as no presumption of merchantability shall attach to such transactions absent explicit contrary agreement. The burden of proof regarding full disclosure rests squarely upon the seller at all times, with any ambiguity resolved strictly against them under established principles of equity and good faith. It is thus imperative that all participants in the magical marketplace adhere scrupulously to these transparency requirements to preserve public safety and maintain confidence in commercial dealings involving arcane technologies. See also § 1001.2 Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets; § 900.4 Identify Fees; Who Pays; § 600.1 Contracts with Non-Casters.

body.heading: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk — Continued
body.text:
§ 1001.7 Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
In transactions involving enchanted items or services, full disclosure of material facts is required to ensure informed consent and prevent fraud. A seller must reveal the true composition, estimated value, and any known risks associated with the item's magical properties. Concealment of these details renders the contract voidable at the buyer's option.

For instance, if a potion purports to enhance strength but contains trace amounts of a toxic alchemical compound, the vendor must disclose this potentially harmful ingredient. Failure to do so constitutes misrepresentation and exposes the seller to liability for resulting injuries or damages. Similarly, when purchasing a cursed blade believed to be a family heirloom, the buyer is entitled to know if the item bears any active enchantments that could affect its performance or safety during use.

The burden of disclosure falls upon the party with superior knowledge regarding the item's condition and capabilities. This often requires independent appraisal by qualified magi or experts before finalizing an agreement. Only through transparent communication can both sides assess whether the deal meets their needs and tolerances for risk.

Moreover, disclosures must be made in a manner reasonably calculated to inform a layperson of pertinent facts. Technical jargon or evasive answers do not suffice. Written documentation is strongly advised to avoid later disputes over what was communicated. In cases where language barriers exist between parties, translation services should be employed to guarantee mutual understanding.

Ultimately, the principle underlying § 1001.7 is one of fair dealing and good faith. By mandating openness about an object's magical nature, the Accords aim to protect all involved from deception and unintended consequences. Whether acquiring a rare scroll or commissioning a complex spellwork project, buyers deserve complete honesty before committing their resources. Sellers likewise benefit from clarifying expectations upfront rather than facing costly litigation down the line. Through diligent adherence to this standard, the marketplace remains vibrant and trustworthy for generations yet unborn."

body.heading: § 1001.7 Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk — Continued
body.text:
Full disclosure under this section requires not only literal accuracy in the spoken tongue but also an explanation of any non-obvious properties that could materially affect the buyer's decision. A seller who states "this amulet is a simple luck charm" while omitting its ability to drain the lifespan of anyone who gazes upon it has failed their duty. Similarly, failing to reveal that a so-called "healing potion" actually accelerates cellular decay constitutes misrepresentation under § 1001.7(a).

The risk associated with an item must be quantified where possible and communicated clearly. A seller offering a "stable mana core" without disclosing its tendency to spontaneously combust at random intervals has not satisfied the disclosure requirement. The buyer's consent is vitiated if they cannot make an informed choice about accepting the risks inherent in their purchase.

In cases where full disclosure would reveal trade secrets or proprietary information, the seller must provide sufficient detail for the buyer to assess value and risk without divulging confidential data. For example, a magic shop may describe an item as "a high-grade component with minor flaws," omitting specific serial numbers or design schematics that identify its origin. This balances transparency with protection of intellectual property rights under § 1001.7(b).

Sellers who knowingly conceal material defects or limitations face severe penalties, including rescission of the transaction and monetary damages. A buyer may void their contract if they can prove they would not have purchased the item had they known the full truth, even if the seller did not explicitly lie. This principle ensures that magical commerce remains fair and trustworthy in an inherently dangerous field.

The burden of disclosure rests squarely on the seller, who is deemed to possess superior knowledge regarding their goods. Buyers are presumed to act with ordinary caution but cannot be expected to detect hidden dangers without proper warnings. Sellers who fail to meet this standard bear responsibility for any resulting harm or loss, whether intentional or negligent in origin.

Through these provisions, § 1001.7 aims to foster transparency and accountability in the magical marketplace, protecting consumers from deceptive practices while respecting legitimate business interests. The goal is a system where all parties can make truly informed decisions about their investments and exposures.

body.heading: § 1001.7 Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk — Continued — Continued
body.text: The obligation to disclose extends beyond mere physical description of the enchanted item. The seller must reveal all material facts regarding the object's magical provenance, including any prior enchantments, defacements, or residual curses that may affect its function or safety. Concealment of such information renders the transaction voidable at the option of the buyer upon discovery. This duty persists even when the hazards are latent and not immediately apparent through ordinary inspection. For instance, a seller must inform a purchaser if an item was previously used in dark rituals, as this may induce unpredictable malfunctions or attract parasitic entities. The standard for full disclosure is that of complete candor; half-truths and euphemisms fail to satisfy the statutory requirement. Sellers who violate this provision commit perjury by omission and are subject to disciplinary sanctions up to and including permanent license revocation. Furthermore, any intentional misrepresentation of an item's true nature constitutes fraud under § 1001.1 and exposes the perpetrator to civil damages in addition to criminal penalties. Buyers should exercise due diligence before entering into such agreements, consulting independent appraisers when necessary to verify claims made by vendors. The Guild reserves the right to inspect any disputed article at its discretion to ascertain whether full disclosure was maintained throughout the sales process. Failure of a seller to comply with these obligations shall be deemed gross misconduct warranting immediate expulsion from membership in good standing and possible prosecution for related offenses under applicable laws.

body.heading: § 1001.7 Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk — Continued — Administration
body.text: In cases where an enchanted object proves dangerous or defective after purchase due to undisclosed flaws, the buyer may seek remedies including rescission of the contract, refund of funds paid, or compensatory damages for losses incurred. The burden of proof rests with the aggrieved party to demonstrate that the seller knowingly concealed material defects at the time of sale. However, the Guild will assist in evaluating complex magical items and determining liability based on available evidence. Sellers who routinely engage in deceptive practices may face enhanced penalties and mandatory remedial training before being permitted to resume business operations. The ultimate goal is to foster transparency and trust within the marketplace while protecting consumers from unwitting exposure to harmful artifacts. Through rigorous enforcement of these disclosure mandates, the Autumnwood Accords strive to maintain fair trading standards that benefit all participants in the magical economy. Any seller found guilty of systematic fraud shall be blacklisted across all Guild jurisdictions and barred from operating legally anywhere within the realm. Their actions represent a profound breach of ethical conduct and undermine the integrity of the entire industry. Such individuals must face swift and severe consequences to deter future misconduct and preserve public confidence in enchanted goods. The Guild remains vigilant in its mission to safeguard citizens from predatory vendors who would exploit their ignorance for personal gain at everyone else's expense. Justice shall be served, and wrongdoers held accountable for their transgressions against the spirit of fair trade enshrined herein.

sections.title: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
sections.brief: Lead remains lead for tax until the assay desk agrees.

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
The transmutation of base metals into precious ores, specifically the conversion of lead into gold, is subject to the strict reporting thresholds established by the Archmage Veyra’s treasury oversight. It is a fundamental principle of the Accords that the physical state of an asset determines its tax liability. Therefore, lead remains lead for the purposes of the Guild’s tax and reporting requirements until such time as the official Guild Assay Desk has performed a certified inspection and issued a formal Certificate of Transmutation. Any mage who attempts to move, sell, or hide lead that has been aesthetically "gold-plated" via low-level illusion or minor transmutation without filing a notice of intent shall be subject to fines for tax evasion.

The reporting threshold is triggered the moment a transmutation becomes permanent or semi-permanent. Temporary transmutations intended for artistic display or theatrical use do not require filing, provided the duration is less than one lunar cycle and the gold does not enter the commercial stream. However, should the gold be used as a medium of exchange, it must be declared immediately. The Guild maintains a "Lead Status" on all uncertified heavy metals; until the Assay Desk signs off, any gold-colored substance is legally classified as lead for the purpose of calculating the Innovators' research surcharges. This prevents the illicit laundering of base metals through "experimental" transmutation labs.

Mages found attempting to bypass the Assay Desk by selling "fresh" gold directly to non-Guild members are in violation of the Accord’s transparency statutes. Such actions are viewed as a circumvention of the Guild’s role as the primary mediator of magical wealth. If a transaction involves a significant volume of transmuted ore, the Aegis Magi may be dispatched to verify the transmutation’s stability before the sale is finalized. See § 1001.13 regarding the use of extra-dimensional storage for such materials.

body.heading: § 1001.8 Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
Whereas certain base metals may undergo transmutation into precious alloys or pure substances through arcane intervention, the Accords establish strict protocols for such transactions to prevent market manipulation and illicit enrichment. Specifically, any instance where lead is converted directly to gold—or any other base metal transformed into a high-value commodity via magical means—shall be considered a reportable event under § 1001.8(a).

The burden of reporting rests upon the caster responsible for the transmutation. Failure to file an immediate declaration with the Accords Desk within forty-eight (48) hours constitutes a Class A violation subject to severe penalties, including permanent license revocation and monetary fines ranging from one thousand to five thousand gold pieces per occurrence (§ 1001.8(b)). The reporting form must detail the precise nature of the transformation performed, the materials used, the magical techniques employed, and any potential side effects or risks associated with the procedure (§ 1001.8(c)).

In addition to standard licensing fees, a special assessment equal to fifteen percent (15%) of the fair market value of the resulting gold shall be levied upon successful lead-to-gold conversions. This tax serves both as compensation for the Desk's oversight services and as a deterrent against frivolous or unethical experimentation with fundamental transmutation arts (§ 1001.8(d)). Refusal to pay the assessed fee may result in immediate suspension of all magical privileges until compliance is achieved, at which point normal processing resumes pursuant to § 200.4.

The Accords Desk reserves the right to conduct random audits and inspections of transmutation laboratories and workshops to ensure adherence to these regulations. Non-compliance discovered during such examinations shall trigger an expedited investigation under relevant provisions of Title VIII, with potential sanctions escalated accordingly (§ 1001.8(e)). All reports submitted pursuant to this section remain confidential except as necessary for regulatory review, in accordance with § 700.2 governing scrying and privacy rights.

This provision is intended solely to regulate the economic implications of magical transmutation and does not prohibit or restrict the practice itself when conducted lawfully within licensed facilities. Any doubts regarding interpretation shall be resolved by reference to the spirit of the Accords as expounded upon in official commentary and case law (§ 1001.8(f)). Violations of this section are hereby designated as a felony under applicable local statutes, subject to enhanced penalties up to double those normally prescribed for similar offenses committed outside the scope of these regulations (§ 1001.8(g)).

See also § 300.2 regarding the classification and restriction of transmutation-related arts; § 900.5 concerning false provenance claims involving magical items; and § 600.1 for provisions pertaining to contracts entered into by non-casters in relation to spellcasting services. Any ambiguities arising from this section shall be construed strictly against any party seeking to evade compliance obligations, consistent with established principles of magical jurisprudence (§ 1001.8(h)).

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold Conversion Reporting Threshold
body.text:
§ 1001.8 Lead-to-Gold Conversion and Reporting Obligations

A fundamental principle underpinning the integrity of the Accords' economic framework is the strict prohibition against unauthorized transmutation of base metals into precious alloys or bullion, a practice known as "lead-to-gold" conversion. Such acts constitute both fraud and an interference with the Guild's regulatory monopoly over magical metallurgy. To enforce this ban effectively, § 1001.8 establishes clear reporting thresholds and procedures for detecting illicit alchemical transactions.

Any mage or entity engaged in commerce involving lead ore, refined lead, gold dust, ingots, coins, or finished goods containing these materials must maintain detailed records of all incoming and outgoing shipments. These logs shall include precise weights, purity levels, assay results, dates of transfer, counterparty identification, and payment methods. Failure to comply with this record-keeping requirement constitutes a prima facie violation warranting immediate investigation by the Aegis Magi.

Furthermore, § 1001.8 mandates that any conversion process resulting in a net gain exceeding two percent must be reported within seven days via Form MM-72, "Lead-to-Gold Activity Report". This report shall detail the quantities of raw materials consumed, the yield produced, the efficiency ratio achieved, and an explanation of the necessity for such operations. The Desk shall review all submissions quarterly to identify patterns suggestive of circumvention schemes or systematic abuse of loopholes.

Mages found guilty of violating § 1001.8 face severe penalties ranging from confiscation of assets and equipment to permanent revocation of licensure. In egregious cases involving large-scale operations, criminal prosecution may ensue under relevant statutes governing economic crime. The Guild retains discretion to impose additional sanctions deemed appropriate to restore market equilibrium and punish bad actors.

This provision embodies the Accords' broader commitment to preventing magical manipulation from undermining societal stability through devious means. By maintaining rigorous oversight of lead-to-gold conversions, the Guild safeguards against inflationary pressures and preserves fair competition among lawful practitioners. All members are expected to uphold these standards diligently, recognizing their vital role in protecting the collective good.

body.heading: § 1001.8 Lead-to-Gold Conversion Reporting Threshold
body.text:
Any caster or entity engaged in the transmutation of base metals into noble substances must file an initial disclosure with the Autumnwood Accords Desk within three business days following completion of said alchemical operation, regardless of whether the resulting product is intended for commercial sale, personal use, or experimental application. This requirement applies equally to both manual and automated conversion processes, including but not limited to artisanal smithing operations and industrial-scale refining facilities utilizing arcane catalysis techniques. Failure to submit timely notification shall constitute a Class C violation subject to standard penalties outlined herein.

Notwithstanding the foregoing disclosure obligation, no further reporting is mandated unless the total market value of successfully converted material exceeds one hundred gold pieces (100 gp), calculated at prevailing exchange rates as determined by the Guild's official assaying division. This threshold exists to balance administrative efficiency with regulatory thoroughness, recognizing that minor alchemical experiments pose negligible risk while large-scale transmutation activities warrant heightened scrutiny for potential market manipulation or illicit fund laundering purposes. Casters exceeding this monetary limit must additionally provide a detailed breakdown of input materials, energy expenditures, and yield percentages alongside their routine filing submission.

The provisions set forth in this section operate independently of any existing tax obligations imposed upon physical commodities under separate statutes. Lead-to-gold conversions remain subject to full taxation until explicitly exempted by the Accords Desk or superseded by newer legislation enacted through proper procedural channels. Consequently, entities engaging in such activities must maintain accurate records sufficient to demonstrate compliance with both alchemical reporting requirements and applicable fiscal liabilities simultaneously.

Casters found willfully evading disclosure obligations shall face escalated sanctions commensurate with the severity of noncompliance, ranging from monetary fines up to two hundred gold pieces for first-time offenses to permanent revocation of licensure for repeat violators. In egregious cases involving substantial sums or evidence of coordinated malfeasance, disciplinary action may proceed directly to a formal Paradox Trial before an impartial panel convened specifically for such matters. All penalties imposed under this section are cumulative and do not preclude concurrent civil liability claims arising from related damages or losses suffered by third parties as a result of negligent conversion practices.

It is hereby declared that the obligations herein constitute a fundamental condition precedent to lawful operation within the jurisdictional bounds of the Autumnwood Accords. No caster shall engage in lead-to-gold transmutation without first ensuring full adherence to all stipulated reporting mandates, thereby safeguarding public welfare and maintaining integrity throughout the magical economy governed by these hallowed agreements. Let this clause stand as a testament to the enduring wisdom of our ancestors who foresaw such necessities long ago.

§ 1001.8 Lead-to-Gold Conversion Reporting Threshold — see also § 200.6 Constructs That Hold a Quill regarding automated compliance mechanisms, § 900.1 Duty to File Before Casting for general filing protocols, and § 300.5 Research Copies of Quiet Items concerning material provenance verification requirements.

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold Conversion Reporting Thresholds
body.text:
§ 1001.8 Lead-to-Gold Conversion Reporting Thresholds

Subsection 1: Lead-to-Gold Conversion Reporting Thresholds

All transactions involving the conversion of lead into gold via arcane means must be reported to the Mages' Guild within seventy-two (72) hours of completion, unless otherwise exempted under § 1001.9. Failure to comply may result in sanctions up to and including temporary suspension of licensure under § 800.1(a)(iv). The reporting obligation applies regardless of whether the transformation was successful or yielded a profit; even failed attempts must be disclosed if they involved licensed practitioners or Guild-regulated materials.

Subsection 2: Exemptions and Special Provisions

Certain limited conversions may be exempt from immediate reporting, provided prior written authorization is obtained from the Conservators' Oversight Committee. Such approvals are typically granted only for academic research purposes or emergency medical applications where gold-based treatments are unavailable. Any such authorized activity must still undergo post-completion audit to verify compliance with all safety and containment protocols outlined in Part IV. Unauthorized circumvention of these procedures constitutes gross negligence punishable under § 800.1(d).

Subsection 3: Enforcement Mechanisms

To facilitate oversight, the Guild maintains a centralized registry of all approved lead-to-gold conversion facilities and their operating parameters. Periodic unannounced inspections shall be conducted to ensure adherence to established standards. Violations discovered during these audits may trigger expedited disciplinary proceedings independent of the regular complaint process described elsewhere in this Code. Persistent offenders face escalating penalties ranging from fines calculated as a percentage of illicit gains to permanent revocation of professional credentials.

Subsection 4: Collaborative Investigations

When suspected violations involve multiple parties or cross-jurisdictional elements, affected jurisdictions shall cooperate fully under mutual legal assistance treaties existing between member states. Evidence gathered during joint operations enjoys privileged status unless directly challenged in court proceedings initiated by an aggrieved party. Results of such investigations inform future policy adjustments and risk assessment models employed by the Guild to anticipate emerging threats posed by unregulated alchemical practices.

This provision reflects collective wisdom honed through decades of trial and error, embodying our shared commitment to maintaining order amidst chaos. By adhering strictly to these guidelines, all practitioners contribute meaningfully toward safeguarding societal interests while pursuing noble goals within legally defined boundaries. Let none forget that true mastery lies not in domination over nature but in harmonious coexistence therewith—a principle enshrined throughout this entire compilation of laws designed specifically for our unique circumstances as stewards of magical knowledge."

*End of § 1001.8 Lead-to-Gold Conversion Reporting Thresholds.*

body.heading: § 1001.8 Lead-to-Gold Conversion Reporting Thresholds
body.text:
Any practitioner who engages in the conversion or exchange of lead for gold, whether through alchemical transmutation, magical enhancement, or other means, shall report such transaction to the Guild's Assay Desk within seventy-two hours of completion. Failure to comply with this reporting requirement constitutes a Class A violation and may result in immediate suspension of licensure pending investigation.

The reporting obligation applies regardless of whether the lead-to-gold conversion results in a net profit or loss for the practitioner. The sole metric for compliance is the act itself, not its economic outcome. This provision exists to prevent illicit laundering of illegal gains through seemingly legitimate magical services.

Practitioners seeking to convert lead to gold must first obtain written authorization from the Assay Desk, detailing the intended amount and method of transmutation. Unauthorized attempts at such conversions shall be treated as evidence of criminal intent in any subsequent proceedings. The Guild reserves the right to monitor all reported transactions for suspicious activity patterns indicative of tax evasion or money laundering schemes.

Violations of this section may be subject to civil penalties ranging from monetary fines to permanent revocation of licensure, depending on severity and prior record. Criminal charges may also be initiated in conjunction with disciplinary action under applicable laws. Practitioners are advised that repeated noncompliance will likely result in total expulsion from the Guild's membership rolls without recourse or appeal.

The Assay Desk shall maintain a confidential ledger of all reported lead-to-gold conversions, accessible only to sworn officials. Information contained therein is protected by privilege and may not be disclosed outside legal proceedings absent court order or mutual consent between parties involved. This safeguard ensures that sensitive financial data remains secure while enabling effective oversight of potentially illicit activities.

By establishing clear guidelines for reporting obligations surrounding lead-to-gold transactions, the Guild seeks to balance regulatory transparency with necessary privacy protections. Adherence to these provisions reflects a commitment to ethical practice within the broader community of spellcasters and alchemists operating under the Autumnwood Accords framework. Failure to abide by such standards invites harsh consequences designed to preserve public trust in our collective endeavors.

sections.title: Polymorph of Coinage
sections.brief: Shape is not denomination.

body.heading: Polymorph of Coinage
body.text:
The Guild hereby clarifies the distinction between physical shape and legal denomination. A coin, or any other object intended to serve as a medium of exchange, maintains its denomination based on its recognized legal status, not its physical form. The application of polymorph magic to coinage—be it to change its size, weight, color, or shape—does not alter its underlying value, nor does it grant the user the right to redefine that value. For example, a gold sovereign reshaped into the likeness of a dragon remains a gold sovereign; it does not become "dragon-tender."

Any attempt to use polymorph magic to create "custom" denominations or to deceive others regarding the quantity of currency held is a violation of the financial fraud statutes. This includes the practice of "stretching" a single coin into multiple smaller coins through spatial manipulation or physical expansion. Such acts are considered a manipulation of the Guild's economic stability. Mages who engage in the production of polymorph coinage for the purpose of defrauding the public shall be referred to the Paradox Trial for the determination of suitable sanctions.

Furthermore, the Guild does not recognize "artistic" denominations. If a mage produces a coin that is enchanted to look like a different currency but retains the value of the original, it must be clearly marked as a "Commemorative Polymorph." If the mage intends to use the coin as actual tender, it must meet the standard dimensions and weight requirements of the Midlands' currency. Shape is not denomination; any mage who attempts to argue otherwise shall be fined for "Arcane Aestheticism" and required to attend a seminar on the importance of fiscal uniformity.

body.heading: § 1001.9 Polymorph of Coinage and Tender Value
body.text:
It is declared that the magical transformation of base coinage into gold or silver, known as polymorphing, does not alter the legal tender status of the underlying currency unit for purposes of debt satisfaction. A debtor may discharge an obligation by offering a sum of common metal coins equal in face value to the amount owed, even if those coins have been previously transmuted through arcane means. The creditor shall accept such payment without prejudice and may not assert any claim regarding the metaphysical taint or magical residue present upon the offered tender. This principle is rooted in the fundamental concept that money serves as a symbol of value rather than an object of intrinsic worth, and thus its physical composition remains irrelevant to contractual fulfillment.

The prohibition against using polymorphed coins for speculative trading or profit-seeking activities stands unaffected by this ruling. While such items may satisfy debt obligations, they remain subject to all other restrictions placed upon altered currency under the Accords. Any attempt to market or sell polymorphed coinage directly violates § 1001.6 regarding the sale of prohibited magical artifacts. Furthermore, possession of large quantities of transformed money by a single individual raises concerns regarding potential illicit activity and may warrant investigation by Aegis Magi in accordance with standard procedures for suspicious financial behavior.

In cases where the debtor fails to provide appropriate tender within a reasonable time after demand, default interest shall accrue at triple the normal rate until full satisfaction is achieved. This enhanced penalty serves as both deterrent and compensation for the additional burdens placed upon the creditor by having to procure alternative means of payment while awaiting resolution of the dispute. The burden of proof rests with the party alleging breach to demonstrate that valid tender was refused or delayed without justifiable cause.

The Desk emphasizes that these provisions are intended solely to facilitate fair commercial transactions and prevent exploitation of magical phenomena for fraudulent ends. They do not constitute a general license for citizens to engage in unauthorized alteration of currency, which remains strictly prohibited under § 1001.2 except as specifically permitted by written authority from the Guild Master or his duly appointed delegates. Violation of this clause may result in severe sanctions including permanent revocation of licensure and imprisonment at the discretion of the presiding official.

This interpretation is binding upon all persons within Autumnwood jurisdiction unless expressly superseded by subsequent legislation enacted through proper channels of governance. Questions regarding application to particular circumstances shall be referred to the Arcane Judiciary for determination based on facts presented under oath. Failure to comply with these directives may lead to escalated enforcement actions as deemed necessary to uphold the integrity of our shared economic system and protect vulnerable members of society from predatory practices predicated upon arcane deception.

see § 1001.6 Sale of Prohibited Items; see § 200.3 Temporary Mouths for analogies regarding limited-use permissions; under § 1.4 Persons Bound, all citizens must adhere to these regulations regardless of personal beliefs or affiliations. The Desk reserves the right to amend this interpretation as circumstances warrant upon notice and opportunity for hearing.

body.heading: § 1001.9 Polymorph of Coinage and Tender Value — Continued
body.text: The transformation of coinage through spellcraft, whether intentional or incidental, shall not alter the nominal value established by the Crown's minting authority. Under § 1001.2 Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets, the casting of polymorphic enchantments upon currency is strictly forbidden except under license from the Autumnwood Accords Desk. A licensed caster may employ such magic solely to facilitate the exchange rate conversion specified in their permit, with all proceeds deposited into a designated escrow account for audit by the Guild's Treasury Section. Unauthorized transmutation of coinage constitutes both a violation of this section and a breach of § 1001.5 Material Alteration of Traded Goods, subjecting the offender to immediate suspension and potential expulsion from licensure. Furthermore, any dispute arising from altered currency shall be resolved by reference to the original face value prior to modification, unless evidence proves otherwise under oath. This provision ensures the integrity of monetary transactions while accommodating legitimate magical practices within the bounds of law. See also § 1001.7 Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk; § 300.2 Necromancy; Unsanctioned Arts.

body.heading: Polymorphed Coins and the Integrity of Tender
body.text:
§ 1001.9 Polymorphed Coins and the Integrity of Tender — Continued

Where polymorph magic alters the physical form or composition of currency without changing its nominal value, such coins remain valid tender upon presentation to a merchant or debtor. However, any attempt to pass off a transformed coin as unaltered may constitute fraud under § 1001.1 and subject the caster to disciplinary action for misrepresentation of magical effects. The Guild reserves the right to verify the authenticity of disputed currency through arcane inspection, at which point the burden of proof shifts to the possessor to demonstrate lawful acquisition and modification.

The use of polymorph spells on coinage is strictly prohibited except in cases where the transformation is necessary for safe transport or preservation of valuable items. Even then, the original denomination must remain clearly visible or retrievable without damaging the spell's integrity. Merchants may refuse acceptance of altered coins at their sole discretion and are not obligated to provide change or credit in such instances. Any loss resulting from reliance on a defaced coin shall be borne by the presenting party unless proven otherwise through independent appraisal.

This regulation stands separate from statutes governing counterfeit production, which address illicit creation of false currency rather than legitimate modification thereof. Both offenses carry severe penalties including permanent sealing under § 800.3 and potential extradition to local authorities for prosecution under civil code. The Desk maintains a list of approved transformation techniques that preserve the essential identity of the object while allowing for practical utility in trade or storage contexts. Violations may result in suspension of licensure until compliance is demonstrated through certified testing protocols administered by accredited investigators.

For further guidance on acceptable practices regarding magical alteration of personal property, consult § 300.2(c)(iv) and relevant case law including *Veyra v. Brightspark*, 14 A.W. 89 (Autumnwood Cir. 2076). The Guild encourages responsible innovation within established parameters to ensure continued prosperity and safety for all citizens subject to these accords."

"see § 1001.2 Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets; see § 300.2 Unsanctioned Arts; see § 800.3 Seal of Silence"

body.heading: § 1001.9 Polymorphed Currency and Commercial Integrity
body.text:
§ 1001.9 addresses the complex interplay between transformative magic and monetary systems, specifically when polymorphic effects alter coinage in circulation or storage. The fundamental principle underpinning this provision is that all tender remains subject to the original design specifications of the issuing authority, regardless of subsequent magical modifications. Any alteration affecting weight, diameter, composition, surface markings, or numismatic integrity renders such currency void ab initio, as it no longer faithfully represents the sovereign's seal and promise.

The Desk has observed a disturbing trend wherein rogue practitioners utilize polymorph spells to artificially inflate coin value by transforming base metals into precious alloys mid-transaction. While such acts may temporarily yield illicit profit, they ultimately undermine the stability of regional economies and violate the sanctity of standard tender. To counter this menace, § 1001.9 mandates that any party receiving altered currency must immediately cease payment upon discovery and notify local Aegis Magi for investigation. Failure to comply exposes both recipient and dispenser to joint liability for fraud and forgery under §§ 1001.4–1001.6.

Furthermore, the prohibition extends beyond mere visual deception; even subtle shifts in atomic arrangement that alter density or conductivity constitute actionable tampering. Advanced spectroscopic analysis employed by Guild inspectors can detect these microscopic discrepancies with near-perfect accuracy. Any merchant found accepting polymorphed coins faces automatic revocation of licensure and permanent ban from regulated commerce, regardless of subjective intent. The burden of proof rests solely upon the accused to demonstrate good faith reliance on outward appearance—a standard rarely met given the ubiquity of magical augmentation in modern society.

In cases where altered currency enters the financial system en masse, such as during coordinated heists or border crossings, heightened enforcement measures shall be activated under § 1001.9(b). This includes mandatory suspension of all transactions involving affected denominations until full audit is complete, followed by potential implementation of temporary metal detectors at entry points to sensitive facilities. Businesses refusing compliance risk seizure of assets and imprisonment for obstruction of justice. The Desk retains sole discretion to lift restrictions once verification confirms widespread integrity of remaining tender.

Finally, § 1001.9 expressly forbids the creation or possession of "counterfeit standards"—magical devices designed to permanently modify coinage properties without detection. Manufacture, sale, or use of such contraband instruments carries penalties exceeding those for ordinary forgery, reflecting their capacity to destabilize entire markets through engineered inflation or deflation. Violators shall be prosecuted as organized criminals and subject to lifetime disqualification from any trade involving monetary exchange. The Guild views these threats with zero tolerance, pledging relentless pursuit until commercial purity is fully restored across all jurisdictions under its watch.

body.heading: § 1001.9 Polymorphed Coinage and Commercial Integrity
body.text:
It shall be unlawful for any caster or their agent to knowingly introduce into commerce coinage that has been subjected to polymorphic alteration, whether by magical means or otherwise. Such coins, regardless of their apparent denomination or visual resemblance to valid tender, possess no legal value and are deemed worthless in all transactions. The introduction of altered currency constitutes a serious breach of public trust and undermines the integrity of the economic system.

To establish violation under this section, it need only be shown that the accused had actual knowledge or constructive notice of the coin's polymorphed state prior to its circulation. Constructive notice may be inferred from circumstantial evidence including but not limited to: unusual weight discrepancies; inconsistent surface textures or temperatures; anomalous magnetic properties; failure to bear expected mint marks; or receipt of such currency in exchange for goods or services rendered. The burden of proof rests upon the accuser to demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the defendant knowingly facilitated the dissemination of invalid tender.

Upon conviction, offenders shall be subject to immediate forfeiture of all illicitly obtained gains and penalties ranging from monetary fines equivalent to ten times the face value of the altered coins to imprisonment for periods not exceeding one year or both, at the discretion of the adjudicating authority. Repeat offenses may result in escalated sanctions including permanent revocation of casting licenses and registration as a professional criminal under § 1205.6. Furthermore, any entity found complicit in the production, distribution, or acceptance of polymorphed coinage shall be held jointly and severally liable for all resulting damages suffered by third parties relying upon the authenticity of such tender in good faith.

This provision is enacted to safeguard the reliability of monetary exchange within the realm and prevent exploitation of magical technologies to devalue official currency. By criminalizing the use of altered coins, the Accords seek to maintain public confidence in traditional forms of payment while acknowledging the potential for abuse inherent in advanced arcane applications. Enforcement of this clause shall be a priority concern for all regulatory bodies charged with upholding the letter and spirit of these laws.

In cases where polymorphed coinage is discovered during routine inspection or audit procedures, seizing officials are directed to promptly notify both their superiors and representatives from the relevant financial institutions for coordinated action. All confiscated items must be inventoried meticulously and stored securely pending further investigation or disposition as ordered by the presiding officer. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in disciplinary measures against responsible personnel under applicable administrative codes.

The prohibitions herein apply without limitation to any form of altered currency including but not restricted to gold pieces, silver coins, copper pennies, credit chits, digital tokens, or any other medium of exchange recognized by law. Nothing contained in this section shall be construed to diminish the protections afforded bona fide holders who unknowingly received and attempted to utilize polymorphed tender prior to discovery of its illicit nature. Such individuals remain fully entitled to seek restitution from those responsible for introducing invalid funds into circulation, subject only to standard statutes of limitation governing civil actions.

It is hereby declared that violation of this article shall constitute a felony punishable under the full extent of applicable penalties provisions contained herein and elsewhere within these Accords. Courts are urged to impose stringent sanctions on convicted offenders to serve as a deterrent against future infractions and thereby preserve the stability and fairness of commercial dealings throughout our shared domain.
