Defendants charged under this section shall be entitled to call expert witnesses to testify as to whether their actions constituted a Layered Transfiguration Scheme or merely coincidental use of multiple spells. The standard of proof remains high: clear and convincing evidence that the accused acted with deceptive intent is required before sanctions may be imposed.

In cases where layered schemes are uncovered, penalties shall be calibrated to reflect both the complexity of the operation and any resulting harm to public safety or economic stability. Aggravating factors include prior violations, refusal to cooperate with investigation, or evidence that similar activities were conducted on a broader scale. Mitigating circumstances may include voluntary disclosure before discovery by authorities, full restitution of losses incurred, and genuine remorse demonstrated through corrective action.

The provisions herein are intended to close loopholes exploited by cunning mages seeking to skirt the spirit if not the letter of the law. By targeting the methodology rather than just the outcome, this section ensures that no evasive tactic can render transfiguration magic beyond regulatory reach. It represents a fundamental shift in enforcement philosophy, emphasizing proactive oversight over reactive punishment.

This clause shall be construed liberally to encompass all forms of deceptive magical practice, now or later developed. The Desk reserves authority to issue additional guidance as needed to clarify its application in evolving contexts. All persons subject to these Accords are hereby put on notice that any attempt to game the system through layered operations will meet with swift and severe consequences. Compliance is not optional—it is mandatory for all licensed practitioners operating within Autumnwood's jurisdictional boundaries.

body.heading: § 1001.15 Layered Transfiguration Schemes — Continued — Continued
body.text:
§ 1001.15 Layered Transfiguration Schemes, in the sense applied herein, refers to those complex arrangements wherein magical effects are compounded or nested such that their individual components may not be readily discernible upon casual inspection. A classic example involves a gemstone enchanted first with an illusion of wealth, then concealed within a bag-of-holding spell, which is itself disguised as a mundane trinket worn by the owner. To a novice observer—or even to a clerk unfamiliar with such stratagems—the object appears innocuous; yet its true value may exceed that of the desk upon which it rests.

The Accords treat these layered schemes not merely as curiosities, but as potential instruments of fraud and evasion. For where one can see only surface appearances, the cunning mage perceives hidden depths. And in those depths lies the capacity to mislead, deceive, or conceal assets from proper taxation or seizure. Henceforth, all such arrangements shall be deemed "material facts" subject to full disclosure prior to any transaction involving magical goods or services. Failure to reveal their existence may constitute grounds for revocation of licensure, and in cases of deliberate obfuscation designed to avoid liability, punitive damages may also be awarded at the discretion of the Desk.

It bears emphasis that this provision does not prohibit innovation per se; rather, it mandates transparency where ambiguity threatens public interest. A well-documented enchantment applied openly for legitimate purposes remains fully compliant with existing statutes. The prohibition arises only when the very nature of the scheme renders its true scope unknowable until too late. Let no one mistake caution for censorship—we encourage boldness within bounds, not recklessness under cover of secrecy.

Accordingly, every licensee is charged with exercising due diligence in both creating and disclosing any layered transfiguration schemes involving their property or services. Inquiries regarding specific applications shall be directed to the Conservators' Office of Magical Standards, which maintains a registry of approved designs for reference purposes only. Unauthorized experimentation falls strictly outside the scope of this Code, regardless of intent or outcome. The Desk retains sole authority to determine whether any given arrangement complies with applicable laws and regulations as they may evolve over time.

See also § 1001.3 Valuation After Alteration (regarding disclosure obligations); § 900.2 Reporting of Material Enchantments (for related filing requirements); and Part II, Chapter 4 (on research permits for novel constructs). Violators subject to sanctions under §§ 800.1–800.5 as appropriate.

body.heading: § 1001.15 Layered Transfiguration Schemes — Continued — Administration
body.text:
§ 1001.15 Layered Transfiguration Schemes — Continued

A particularly insidious form of fraud involves the application of multiple, compounding transmutation spells to a single item, each designed to obscure the true nature and value of the underlying object. For example, a base material such as lead may first be transmuted into gold via a primary spell, then further enchanted with an illusionist's trick to appear unblemished and lustrous despite potential flaws or wear. Additional layers of magic might include a memory charm to erase evidence of previous alterations, a clone created solely for the purpose of holding the original item while the fraudulent article is marketed under false pretenses, and finally a seal of silence cast upon all witnesses to prevent them from testifying against the perpetrator.

The Desk takes strong exception to such elaborate schemes, viewing them as an egregious abuse of arcane power for purely nefarious ends. Under § 1001.6, any endowment or gift containing hidden enchantments must be fully disclosed before acceptance; failure to do so constitutes material misrepresentation and grounds for immediate revocation of the transaction. Moreover, the cumulative effect of multiple spells applied in succession often exceeds safe operational limits, posing a genuine threat to public safety should the item later come into competent hands. The Guild makes no distinction between simple forgery and complex transfiguration fraud; both are treated as serious breaches of trust and subject to full penal sanctions under Title VIII.

Clerks are directed to scrutinize all high-value transactions with heightened vigilance, particularly those involving enchanted goods or services. Any suspicious circumstances should be promptly reported for investigation by the Aegis Magi, who possess the authority to seize disputed items and interrogate involved parties as needed. The Desk retains broad discretion to impose additional requirements on repeat offenders, ranging from mandatory retraining courses to outright suspension of licensure pending further review. Ultimately, it is incumbent upon every registered caster to uphold the highest standards of integrity in their professional dealings; anything less will not be tolerated under the Autumnwood Accords.

body.heading: § 1001.15 Layered Transfiguration Schemes — Continued — Administration — Continued
body.text: § 1001.15 Layered Transfiguration Schemes — Continued — Administration shall govern the procedural handling of complex, multi-stage transmutation operations involving nested magical effects or sequential alterations to a single object. Such layered schemes present unique challenges for valuation, disclosure, and regulatory compliance, requiring heightened scrutiny from both the Mages' Guild Desk and affected third parties. Under this provision, any party initiating a series of enchantments upon an item must file a detailed Breakdown of Effects with the appropriate regional office prior to commencing work. This document shall enumerate each individual spell or alteration, its intended function, the materials consumed, and the projected final state of the object post-completion. Failure to provide this comprehensive disclosure may result in immediate suspension of all related permits and potential disciplinary action against the responsible caster. Furthermore, any mid-process deviations from the originally filed plan must be reported within forty-eight hours via supplementary filing. Unreported changes that materially alter the risk profile or economic value of the finished product shall constitute grounds for revocation of licensure and imposition of civil penalties up to five times the standard fee schedule. The Mages' Guild retains broad discretion to order independent audits whenever evidence suggests concealment of material facts regarding layered transfiguration activities. Any party sustaining demonstrable loss due to non-compliance with these administrative requirements may bring a direct action for damages before the Accords Desk, without need to exhaust other remedies first. This section operates in conjunction with §§ 1001.3, 1001.6, and 900.2 regarding disclosure obligations and record retention mandates applicable to all magical service providers operating within Guild jurisdiction. Violations may also trigger referral for criminal prosecution under relevant statutes where appropriate. The Desk shall promulgate additional guidance documents as needed to clarify implementation specifics without altering the substantive requirements herein set forth. All provisions of this Article remain fully enforceable notwithstanding any conflicting internal policies or unwritten customs contrary hereto.

sections.title: Gifts That Later Move
sections.brief: A gift with a remaining geas is not a gift.

body.heading: Gifts That Later Move
body.text:
A gift with a remaining geas is not a gift. Under the prevailing statutes of the Autumnwood Accords, a "gift" is defined as a voluntary transfer of magical, physical, or metaphysical property without the expectation of future consideration or the imposition of lingering obligations. When a donor purports to bestow an item upon a recipient, but the item remains bound by a geas, enchantment, or lingering magical tether that dictates the recipient's actions, the transfer is legally categorized as a "conditional conveyance" rather than a gift. Such an act constitutes a violation of the principle of free agency and may be subject to immediate seizure by the Aegis Magi. If the geas is active at the time of transfer, the donor has effectively bypassed the requirements of a formal contract, and the recipient is not entitled to the protections afforded to gift-receivers. See § 1001.6.

Furthermore, the presence of a lingering geas implies a continuing interest of the donor in the object's utility or the recipient's behavior. This is a fundamental breach of the Accords’ guidelines on the movement of magical assets. Any individual seeking to dispose of a geased object as a gift must first undergo a "Purification of Intent" at a recognized Guild station to ensure all ties to the original owner are severed. Failure to do so shall result in the item being declared "Contraband of Bound Origin." In cases where the geas is clandestine—hidden from the recipient by illusion or complex layering—the donor shall be held liable for "Malicious Tethering," a felony under the current Innovator-Conservator mediation.

The Accords Desk maintains that a gift must be a clean break. If a hat, for instance, begins to bill its wearer for "maintenance" or "protection" after being gifted, it is not a gift but an endowment or a hidden lease. The legal fiction of the gift is dissolved the moment a new obligation is detected. Any party attempting to argue that the geas was a "feature" of the gift is barred from such defense unless the geas was explicitly disclosed in a written deed of transfer. For the purposes of the Paradox Trial, any mage who uses a geased gift to compel a peer into an unauthorized action shall be treated as if they had directly cast the compulsion themselves. See § 800.2.

body.heading: Relics; Chain of Title
body.text:
Provenance, Quiet List relics. All relics of significant arcane magnitude, historical weight, or cultural importance must possess a clear and unbroken chain of title as recognized by the Accords Desk. A relic is defined as any object that has been the focus of a major magical event, a seat of power for a recognized lineage, or an artifact of the Quiet List. For items originating from the Quiet List, the chain of title is inherently restricted; while the existence of such items is not a matter of public record, their movement between private collectors and Guild-sanctioned vaults must be documented via "Shadow Ledgers." Any relic whose provenance is obscured by more than three generations of ownership, or which lacks a verified signature from a known artisan or mage of standing, shall be subject to a "Provenance Inquiry."

During a Provenance Inquiry, the Aegis Magi may seize the artifact for a period not to exceed thirty days to verify its history. If the artifact is found to be a product of the Iron Mandate or the Regal Empire’s illicit seizures, it shall be confiscated immediately. Furthermore, relics associated with the Silver Flame or the Cosmic Jesters are subject to heightened scrutiny and may be declared "Hostile Assets" if their chain of title involves any recognized agents of these factions. The Accords Desk does not recognize "finders keepers" as a valid basis for the acquisition of relics; any item of power found in the wild must be reported to the nearest Conservator outpost for appraisal and registration.

The Quiet List, while not a public catalogue, serves as the primary registry for items that pose a risk to the stability of the Midlands. Relics held by the public that are found to be on the Quiet List without proper authorization shall be placed under "Active Custodianship." Owners of such relics are granted the right to possess them but are strictly prohibited from displaying, selling, or lending them to non-Guild entities. Any breach of these restrictions shall result in the immediate revocation of the owner's right of possession and the initiation of a Paradox Trial to determine if the relic’s misuse constitutes a threat to the Accords. See § 800.2.

body.heading: Curse as Warranty Disclaimer
body.text:
A curse is not 'as is' unless disclosed. In the commerce of magical artifacts and enchanted goods, the "As Is" clause is frequently invoked by vendors to absolve themselves of liability for the inherent properties of an item. However, the Autumnwood Accords explicitly state that a curse—defined as a persistent, harmful, or restrictive magical effect intended to afflict the owner or user—does not qualify as an "inherent property" for the purpose of warranty disclaimer. If a vendor sells a cursed object without a prominent, magically-detectable warning, they are in violation of the Accords. The burden of disclosure lies with the seller; the buyer is not required to possess advanced scrying capabilities to identify a hidden curse.

Any contract of sale that includes a "Curse as Warranty Disclaimer" is considered null and void. The presence of a curse is viewed as a defect in the item's utility, much like a structural flaw in a physical building. If a buyer discovers a curse that was not disclosed at the time of sale, they are entitled to a full refund of the purchase price, plus any "Restoration Fees" incurred to cleanse the object. The seller may be further fined for "Negligent Enchantment," particularly if the curse is of a nature that causes permanent physical or mental harm. The Aegis Magi are authorized to perform "Truth-Binding" on vendors who claim they were unaware of the curse's existence.

For the purposes of the Accords Desk, a "curse" is distinguished from a "volatile enchantment." A volatile enchantment is a known risk associated with high-level magic (such as a rift-prone focus) and may be sold with a standard warning. A curse, however, is a targeted malicious effect. Therefore, while a mage may sell a staff that has a chance of exploding (volatile), they may not sell a staff that actively drains the user's life force (curse) without a specific, notarized disclosure. Failure to provide such disclosure shall result in the immediate suspension of the vendor’s Guild license and a mandatory appearance before the Conservators. See § 800.1.

body.heading: Blessing of a Competing Vendor
body.text:
A blessing sold against a rival is advertising, then fraud if it binds. The Accords recognize the right of mages to engage in the trade of blessings, which are categorized as "Positive Efficacy Charms." However, when a blessing is specifically designed to provide a mechanical or magical advantage over a competitor’s product—for example, a blessing that causes a rival’s shield to shatter upon contact—it is classified as "Aggressive Advertising." Such blessings must be clearly labeled as "Competitive Efficacy" and are subject to a higher licensing fee. If a blessing is sold with the intent to sabotage a rival's goods, the seller must ensure that the effect is localized and does not cause collateral damage to the general populace or the Midlands' infrastructure.

Fraud occurs when a blessing sold against a rival contains a "Binding Clause" or a "Hidden Malus." If a mage sells a "Loyalty Blessing" for a customer that secretly binds the customer to the mage’s own services while simultaneously degrading the customer's ability to use any other merchant's products, this is a violation of the Accords. The transition from "Aggressive Advertising" to "Fraud" occurs at the moment the magic exerts unauthorized control over the recipient’s agency or financial independence. The Accords Desk views the use of magic to create "Monopolistic Bindings" as a severe violation of the principles of fair trade and magical stability.

Any party found guilty of such fraud shall be subject to a Paradox Trial. The punishment for "Binding Fraud" is often the "Seal of Silence" on the offending mage's commercial magic, preventing them from selling any blessings for a period of no less than ten years. Furthermore, the mage may be required to issue a "Public Rectification," a magically-broadcasted apology to all affected customers. The Aegis Magi are tasked with monitoring the marketplaces of the Midlands to ensure that blessings remain tools of protection and enhancement rather than instruments of economic enslavement. See § 800.3.

body.heading: § 1101.1 Gifts That Later Move; Relics and Chain of Title
body.text: A gift or donation made under duress, mistake, or ignorance is voidable at the donor's election within one solar cycle. See §§ 2.5 (Coercion), 3.4 (Mental Incapacity). A recipient who takes title with actual knowledge of a defect in the grantor's authority assumes the risks of future discovery. Id. Conversely, bona fide purchasers without notice acquire good title free of prior encumbrances, subject to any reserved rights expressly retained by the donor. § 1102.3. The rule of constructive notice applies where public records exist; otherwise, actual knowledge is required to bind a successor in interest. See §§ 501.2 (Public Records), 604.1 (Estoppel). A curse attached to an object functions as a warranty disclaimer unless expressly negated by the donor's intent. § 1103.5. A blessing conferred by a third party does not validate a defective conveyance absent consideration or ratification. Id. Relics bearing residual enchantments must be disclosed prior to transfer; nondisclosure constitutes fraud and grounds for rescission. § 814.7. The burden of proving a gift was tainted lies with the aggrieved party, who must establish clear and convincing evidence of improper motive or undue influence. See § 902.3 (Burden of Proof). Once title passes cleanly, subsequent claims based on hidden defects are barred unless fraud is proven beyond reasonable doubt. § 1104.1. Exceptions apply where the donor retains a life estate or right of revocation, in which case the grantee holds only a qualified interest subject to termination upon notice. See §§ 712.5 (Life Estates), 809.1 (Revocable Trusts). A gift made in contemplation of death is presumed irrevocable unless shown otherwise by clear evidence of contrary intent at the time of execution. § 1105.4. Any attempt to condition a completed gift on future events fails as against public policy and the donor's vested rights. Id. The doctrine of part performance may cure defects where the recipient has relied substantially to their detriment in good faith. See §§ 608.2 (Reliance), 719.3 (Unjust Enrichment). Ultimately, fairness dictates that gifts should not be undermined by technicalities once title passes and reliance occurs. § 1106.5. This principle balances the donor's autonomy with the recipient's security of transaction, fostering trust in magical commerce. Id. Where doubts arise regarding the nature or validity of a gift, equitable remedies may supplement strict legal rules to achieve justice between the parties. See § 724.1 (Equitable Jurisdiction).

body.heading: § 1101.2 Gifts With Attached Obligations; The Curse as Warranty Disclaimer
body.text:
A gift that carries attached obligations may not be accepted without full knowledge thereof. Where a donor imposes conditions upon the transfer of magical property, those conditions bind the recipient irrespective of subsequent changes in status or possession. This rule ensures that gifts remain true to their original intent and prevents exploitation through circumvention of terms.

The curse accompanying a relic functions as an explicit warranty disclaimer, warning potential recipients of inherent dangers and limitations. Acceptance of such items constitutes agreement to abide by these warnings, regardless of whether the recipient later discovers additional hazards or beneficial properties. This principle protects both donor and donee from unintended consequences arising from incomplete understanding of the item's nature.

Blessings bestowed upon objects by third parties do not negate prior obligations imposed by the original giver. A competitor's benediction may enhance an artifact's capabilities, but it cannot alter the fundamental terms of its transfer. The recipient remains bound by the initial agreement, even if new powers emerge through external intervention. This maintains clarity in contractual relationships and prevents confusion over liability for damages or injuries resulting from blessed items.

sections.title: Relics; Chain of Title
sections.brief: Provenance, Quiet List relics.

body.heading: Relics; Chain of Title
body.text:
The acquisition, transfer, and possession of any artifact of significant thaumaturgical potency, hereafter referred to as a "Relic," shall be governed by the strict requirements of the Chain of Title as established under the Autumnwood Accords. A Relic is defined as any object imbued with persistent magical properties, historical significance, or a lineage of ownership that exceeds three consecutive owners within a single century. To establish a valid Chain of Title, a claimant must provide a documented history of possession that is free from "arcane gaps"—periods of time where the Relic’s location or ownership is unaccounted for by any recognized Guild registry. Any Relic lacking a continuous history of provenance is deemed "Orphaned" and may be subject to seizure by the Aegis Magi for the purpose of public safety and the prevention of unauthorized ritual activation.

Provenance must be verified by a licensed Notary of the Accords Desk. A mere oral history or a personal narrative provided by a seller does not constitute a legal Chain of Title; as stated in § 900.5, a story is not a chain of title. The claimant must present physical evidence of transfer, such as signed Deeds of Relinquishment, notarized Wills of the deceased, or verified records of auction. In instances where a Relic was obtained through non-standard means, such as "discovery" in wild zones or ruins, the claimant must provide a Certificate of Discovery, which includes a survey of the site to ensure no local treaties or sovereign boundaries were violated. Failure to provide such documentation shall result in the Relic being classified as "Unsanctioned," rendering it illegal to transport or trade within the Midlands.

Special provisions apply to items designated on the Quiet List. Any Relic identified as a Quiet List asset is subject to heightened secrecy and restricted movement. The Chain of Title for a Quiet List Relic must be held in a sealed, magically-locked vault accessible only by the owner and the Archmage Veyra. Public disclosure of the existence of a Quiet List Relic, or any attempt to register its Chain of Title in a public ledger, shall be grounds for immediate prosecution. See § 300.3 for specific procedures regarding the non-public listing of such items. Furthermore, any Relic whose provenance involves the Regal Empire, the Iron Legion, or the Silver Flame is subject to immediate confiscation and "Sanction and Seal" procedures, as these entities are deemed hostile to the Accord's jurisdiction.

Mages who possess Relics without a verified Chain of Title are prohibited from utilizing the Relic's primary functions for any public-facing purpose. This includes, but is not limited to, the use of Relics in street duels, public demonstrations, or the charging of local mana-grids. Should a Relic be found to have a fractured Chain of Title due to a lapse in documentation, the owner may apply for a "Restoration of Title" through a formal petition to the Conservators. This process requires a full audit of the object’s history and may involve a fee to the Aegis Magi to cover the costs of investigative magical tracing. If the petition is denied, the Relic shall be held in escrow by the Guild until such time as a valid Chain of Title can be produced or the item is declared a public hazard and subsequently neutralized.

body.heading: § 1101.2 Relics; Chain of Title Provenance and Authenticity
body.text:
Every relic, artifact, or enchanted object traded within the Accords must bear an unbroken chain of title tracing its origin to a lawful source. See §§ 300.4 Specimen Custody, 900.5 False Provenance. Any item lacking proper documentation shall be deemed contrabunt and subject to seizure under § 800.1 Discipline, Range of Sanctions. The burden of proof rests upon the seller to demonstrate clear ownership prior to transaction. Failure to do so constitutes a prima facie case for fraud under § 1001.1 Financial Fraud and Manipulation Generally.

Relics found in the wild or salvaged from ruins require immediate reporting to the nearest Aegis Magi detachment within seventy-two hours. See § 900.2 Reporting of Material Enchantments, Duties of Discoverers. Unregistered items shall be confiscated pending investigation by the Conservators or Innovators as appropriate. Possession without authority is punishable as possession of stolen goods under applicable law. This provision aims to prevent illicit trafficking and ensure all magical artifacts enter the market through regulated channels.

The Desk reserves the right to require additional background checks, security clearances, or character references for high-value transactions involving particularly potent relics. See § 200.5 Guest Casters, Enhanced Vetting Procedures. Sellers must disclose any known defects, curses, or unstable properties of the item in writing before finalizing the sale. Concealment of material facts renders the contract voidable at the option of either party and may result in disciplinary action for professional misconduct.

Chain of title documentation must include original purchase receipts, transfer deeds, appraisal certificates, and any relevant magical attestation scrolls. Copies shall be filed with the Guild Records Office pursuant to § 900.3 Record Retention requirements. Failure to maintain adequate records may lead to denial of future licensure or suspension of existing privileges under § 200.4 Suspension and Lapse. This rigorous oversight ensures accountability throughout the lifecycle of every magical commodity transacted within our jurisdiction.

See also §§ 1001.5 Material Alteration of Traded Goods, 1001.7 Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk, for related provisions regarding seller obligations. Under § 1001.4 Illusion-Based Fraud, any attempt to misrepresent the nature or capabilities of a relic shall be treated as aggravated fraud carrying enhanced penalties. The Desk maintains a database of known cursed items and dangerous artifacts that pose special risks to unsuspecting buyers. This resource is available upon request to licensed practitioners for reference during due diligence investigations.

Relics constitute an integral component of our magical economy and demand vigilant stewardship by all participants. By adhering strictly to these provenance requirements, we protect both consumers and the Guild's reputation from exploitation by rogue elements seeking profit through deception or malice alone. The preservation of lawful commerce depends upon collective commitment to transparency, honesty, and ethical dealing in all matters pertaining to enchanted goods and services offered under our watchful gaze forevermore.

body.heading: § 1101.2 Relics; Chain of Title Provenance and Authenticity Verification of Orig
body.text:
Under this section, the Guild establishes rigorous protocols for verifying the provenance and authenticity of relics and artifacts submitted to its registry. All claimed items must be accompanied by a detailed chain of title, demonstrating unbroken ownership from original acquisition to present possession. Failure to provide adequate documentation will result in immediate rejection of the submission without prejudice to future applications.

Authenticity determinations shall be made exclusively by the Guild's Council of Connoisseurs, composed of recognized experts in relevant fields. This body possesses sole authority to adjudicate disputes regarding item classification and value assessment. Their rulings are final and binding on all parties involved. Appeals must be filed within thirty days of initial determination and will be reviewed de novo by an expanded panel selected via random lottery from registered appraisers.

Relics bearing the marks or seals of prohibited organizations shall not be accepted under any circumstances, regardless of stated provenance. This absolute bar applies even where the item appears defaced or otherwise altered to obscure identifying features. The burden of proving lawful acquisition rests entirely upon the submitter; any presumption of legitimacy will be rebutted by mere allegation of taint.

In cases involving disputed ownership claims, the Guild shall act as neutral arbiter pending resolution of underlying controversies through appropriate legal channels. No relic may enter official storage until all competing interests have been fully litigated and exhausted by competent tribunals. The Guild maintains no vested interest in any such disputes and assumes no liability for subsequent litigation arising from its administrative actions alone.

Submitors are further advised that once accepted, relics become the sole property of the Autumnwood Accords Desk and remain subject to all applicable statutes and regulations indefinitely. Unauthorized removal or attempted sale will constitute a felony offense punishable by heavy fines and imprisonment at the discretion of the presiding judge. Violators may additionally face permanent disbarment from practice within Guild jurisdiction.

This comprehensive framework ensures both the integrity of the relic registry and protection against fraud, theft, or illicit trafficking. By maintaining strict control over classified items, the Guild safeguards public safety while facilitating lawful study and appreciation of magical history's most extraordinary artifacts. All provisions herein shall be construed liberally to effectuate these essential purposes.

body.heading: § 1101.2 Relics; Chain of Title Provenance and Authenticity Verification of Orig — Continued
body.text:
Whereas relics and antiquities possess unique historical and monetary value beyond their material composition, the Accords establish rigorous standards to ensure transactional integrity in this specialized market sector. Section 1101.2 mandates that all parties engaged in the trade of artifacts must maintain comprehensive documentation verifying item provenance from initial acquisition through any subsequent transfers or alterations. This chain of title serves both as evidence of legitimate ownership and as a safeguard against fraudulent practices common within the arcane antiquities community.

The Accords require sellers to provide certified appraisal reports detailing artifact composition, age estimation methods utilized, and disclosure of all known repairs or restorations performed upon the item's surface. Buyers must similarly disclose any prior knowledge of defects, damage, or hidden flaws that may affect value assessment. Failure to comply with these documentation obligations renders transactions voidable at the election of either party within thirty (30) days of discovery.

To facilitate accurate valuation and risk assessment, licensed appraisers are authorized under § 1101.2(c) to employ specialized detection technologies including spectral imaging, elemental resonance scanning, and thermal analysis where appropriate. These tools allow for non-intrusive examination revealing subtle traces of alteration or synthetic replication that might escape conventional visual inspection. Results from such examinations must be recorded in the official ledger maintained by the Antiquities Division.

Parties are further obligated to report any suspected forgery or misrepresentation immediately to prevent wider market contamination. Unsubstantiated accusations may lead to disciplinary proceedings under § 1200, while verified fraud warrants criminal charges pursuant to applicable statutory provisions. The Accords emphasize that transparency and honesty remain paramount in maintaining trust within the relic trading ecosystem governed by these regulations.

This provision operates in conjunction with §§ 900-1000 regarding magical item registration, as well as § 700 covering cognitive manipulation techniques relevant to forgery detection. Violations may result in license revocation under § 800 and potential imprisonment for serious offenses threatening public safety or economic stability. By enforcing strict accountability standards, the Autumnwood Accords aim to foster a fair and secure marketplace benefiting all law-abiding participants engaged in this ancient yet profitable pursuit.

body.heading: § 1101.2 Relics; Chain of Title Provenance and Authenticity Verification of Orig — Administration
body.text:
The provisions of this Part regarding the classification of items as relics and the requirements for establishing a clear chain of title are without prejudice to any claims or interests that may exist in such items under other applicable laws, including but not limited to those governing archaeological sites, cultural heritage, and stolen goods. However, it is hereby declared that where an item has been listed on the Quiet List as a relic, the presumption shall be that such listing constitutes prima facie evidence of both its status as a relic and the invalidity of any subsequent transfers or sales thereof, absent proof to the contrary.

Verification of Origin
Any party seeking to establish a valid chain of title for an item classified as a relic must provide satisfactory documentation verifying the original provenance of said item, including but not limited to: (a) official records from the Autumnwood Hall confirming its inclusion on the Quiet List at the time of acquisition; (b) sworn statements from reputable appraisers or historians attesting to the authenticity and historical significance of the item; and (c) a detailed history of ownership tracing back to the original source. Failure to provide such documentation shall result in the immediate revocation of any permits or licenses issued pursuant to this Part, along with imposition of penalties as deemed appropriate by the Desk.

Furthermore, it is expressly forbidden for any individual or entity to knowingly acquire, possess, or traffic in items listed on the Quiet List without first obtaining written permission from the Archmage Sovereign. Violation of this prohibition shall constitute a serious offense punishable by imprisonment not exceeding five years and/or a fine up to one thousand gold crowns per violation. In addition, all profits derived from such illegal activities shall be forfeited to the Guild for reinvestment in lawful endeavors.

The Desk reserves the right to conduct random inspections of facilities known or suspected to house relics at any time without notice, in order to ensure compliance with these provisions. Refusal to submit to such inspection shall constitute a separate violation subject to additional sanctions. It is hereby declared that the protections afforded by this Part extend equally to both natural persons and artificial entities, including but not limited to corporations, partnerships, trusts, and magical constructs capable of holding property rights.

In witness whereof, I have set forth my hand on this ______ day of ____________, in the year of our Lord ____ and the ____ year of the Autumnwood Accords.

"Provenance is everything. Without it, a relic is nothing more than expensive scrap metal to me." - Archmage Theron, Conservators

"I'll pay top dollar for that ancient scroll! Just name your price!" - Janna Brightspark, Innovators

*This regulation aims to protect the integrity of our most valuable artifacts while providing clear guidelines for their legal acquisition and transfer.*

body.heading: § 1101.2 Relics; Chain of Title Provenance and Authenticity Verification of Orig — Oversight
body.text:
§ 1101.2 Relics; Chain of Title Provenance and Authenticity Verification of Orig - Continued

Where a relic's provenance cannot be established with reasonable certainty, the burden shifts to the possessor to demonstrate that acquisition was lawful. Failure to meet this burden results in presumption of illicit origins under § 1101.3(a). The Desk may require independent authentication from qualified experts at the expense of the disputing party. All findings must be recorded and made available for inspection upon written request.

§ 1101.2 Relics; Chain of Title Provenance and Authenticity Verification of Orig - Administration

The Arch-Mage's Office maintains a registry of certified relic appraisers whose determinations shall carry evidentiary weight in all proceedings. Appraisers must adhere strictly to ethical standards set forth in § 405.1 et seq., including avoidance of conflicts of interest and proper disclosure of any financial ties to the parties involved. Regular audits ensure compliance with these obligations. Violations may result in revocation of certification status pursuant to § 406.2.

The Desk further mandates that all relic transactions exceeding a specified monetary threshold be reported within five business days to prevent money laundering or tax evasion schemes (§ 815.7). This requirement applies regardless of whether the exchange occurred domestically or internationally. Reports submitted in good faith shall remain confidential unless subpoenaed by competent authorities. Willful falsification constitutes perjury under § 923.4, subject to enhanced penalties upon conviction.

In cases involving disputed ownership claims between multiple parties, the Desk shall appoint a neutral mediator with expertise in both legal and arcane matters to facilitate resolution outside formal litigation whenever feasible (§ 105.8). Mediation efforts must conclude within thirty days unless extended by mutual agreement. Failure to participate diligently may result in dismissal of one's claim without prejudice. Costs associated with mediation are typically shared equally among disputants unless otherwise ordered by the mediator based on equitable principles and prior conduct.

This comprehensive framework ensures that relics circulate freely yet responsibly, respecting both their historical significance and inherent magical properties while safeguarding public welfare through vigilant oversight mechanisms designed to detect and deter abuse before it escalates beyond containment capabilities possessed even by seasoned practitioners of highest standing within our guild ranks today!

sections.title: Curse as Warranty Disclaimer
sections.brief: A curse is not 'as is' unless disclosed.

body.heading: Curse as Warranty Disclaimer
body.text:
§ 1101.3 Curse as Warranty Disclaimer. The transfer of any enchanted object, relic, or mundane item bearing a lingering metaphysical burden shall not be governed by the standard "as is" clauses of common commerce under the Autumnwood Accords. Specifically, the presence of a curse—defined herein as any persistent, deleterious magical effect intended to harm, hinder, or drain the vitality, sanity, or resources of a subsequent owner—constitutes a material defect in the item's condition. Any merchant, practitioner, or private citizen seeking to divest themselves of a cursed object may not utilize the standard "as is" disclaimer to insulate themselves from liability. If a curse is present and remains undisclosed at the point of sale or transfer, the seller shall be held in breach of the Accords, subject to the penalties outlined in § 1001.5.

Furthermore, the legal distinction between a "dormant" curse and an "active" curse is irrelevant for the purposes of warranty disclosure. If the magical signature of a curse is detectable by a standard sensory appraisal by a licensed Aegis Mage or a certified Conservator, the seller is mandated to provide a full disclosure of the curse’s origin, potency, and duration. Failure to do so constitutes a willful concealment of a hazard. A curse is not "as is" unless the buyer has been explicitly warned of its existence and has voluntarily accepted the risk of its activation. In such cases of explicit disclosure, the seller may be granted immunity from subsequent claims of "hidden defects," provided the disclosure was made in writing or through a binding verbal contract witnessed by a Guild-recognized notary.

The Innovators may argue that certain "reactive" curses—those that only trigger under specific, rare conditions—do not constitute an immediate defect. The Conservators, however, maintain that any potential for harm constitutes a breach of the stability of the local weave. Therefore, for the purposes of the Autumnwood Accords, any curse that possesses the capacity to manifest harm shall be treated as a primary defect. Any attempt to bypass these requirements by claiming the curse is a "feature" of the item's history, rather than a flaw in its current state, shall be viewed as a fraudulent misrepresentation. See § 1001.7 for requirements regarding the disclosure of risk in complex magical assets.

body.heading: Blessing of a Competing Vendor
body.text:
§ 1101.4 Blessing of a Competing Vendor. The use of benevolent magic, specifically "blessings," to actively undermine the commercial interests of a rival entity is strictly regulated as a form of illicit advertising. While the Mages' Guild recognizes the right of practitioners to promote their services, the application of a blessing to an object or person with the express intent of rendering a competitor's product unusable, unappealing, or magically incompatible is prohibited. If a blessing is sold as a service to a customer with the primary purpose of creating a hostile metaphysical environment against a specific rival vendor, such an act shall be classified as unauthorized advertising.

Should such a blessing contain binding components—namely, magic that actively prevents a consumer from utilizing a competitor's goods or creates a persistent magical barrier against a rival’s influence—it shall be elevated from a mere advertising violation to a felony of magical fraud. Under the Accords, a blessing that binds a consumer to a single vendor by magically suppressing the efficacy of all other competing products is considered a violation of the free flow of magical commerce. Such "exclusive bindings" are prohibited unless the vendor can prove a legitimate safety concern or a unique, non-compressive magical synergy that does not infringe upon the consumer's right to seek alternative services.

The Aegis Magi are authorized to seize any artifacts or objects imbued with such "hostile blessings" and may levy heavy fines against the practitioner who cast them. Furthermore, any vendor found to be distributing blessings of this nature shall be barred from Guild certification for a period of no less than five years. This provision ensures that the marketplace remains a space of open competition rather than one governed by magical monopolies or "blessed" coercion. Practitioners are encouraged to seek counsel with the Conservators to ensure their promotional enchantments do not cross the threshold into prohibited binding magic. See § 1001.1 for general principles on financial fraud and manipulation.

body.heading: § 1101.3 Curse as Warranty Disclaimer; Blessing of Competing Vendor
body.text:
A magic item sold under the guise of "as is" remains subject to all standard warranties and representations unless explicitly disclaimed in writing by a licensed appraiser. The mere presence of a curse or flaw does not constitute an adequate disclaimer, especially where such defects materially impair the intended function of the object. Any seller who knowingly conceals known hazards risks treble damages under § 1101.4.

Conversely, when an item is blessed by a competing vendor with protective enchantments, these benefits survive transfer unless specifically negated. Such blessings may include immunity to certain curses, resistance to degradation, or minor utility enhancements. The buyer stands in privity with both the original caster and subsequent owners, entitled to enforce these protections against any party interfering with their use.

This section supersedes conflicting terms in private contracts only where those terms violate public policy or explicit statutory prohibitions. Parties may agree to modify standard warranties provided they do so knowingly and voluntarily, without duress or fraud. Any ambiguity regarding the scope of a disclaimer shall be construed most strongly against the drafter.

See also § 1001.8 Lead-to-Gold for valuation standards when magical artifacts enter commerce; § 300.5 Research Copies of Quiet Items for exceptions regarding laboratory specimens; and § 200.6 Constructs That Hold a Quill for automated transactions involving sentient beings. Under § 700.5 Clone as Duplicate Claimant, multiple ownership claims arising from duplication shall be resolved according to established precedence rules detailed therein.

The principles outlined herein reflect the Guild's enduring commitment to fair trade practices and consumer protection within the magical economy. By setting clear expectations for both sellers and buyers, these provisions foster trust and stability in an inherently volatile marketplace. All parties are urged to familiarize themselves thoroughly with this section before engaging in any transaction involving enchanted goods.

body.heading: § 1101.3 Curse as Warranty Disclaimer; Blessing of Competing Vendor — Continued
body.text:
A magical item sold or transferred by the owner, whether gratuitously or for value, carries with it an implied warranty that it is free from any harmful enchantments known to the seller at the time of sale. This obligation applies regardless of whether the transfer was express or silent, oral or written. Failure to disclose a curse renders the transaction voidable at the option of the buyer, who may seek rescission and damages for reliance losses suffered in good faith belief that the item was safe.

Conversely, if a seller expressly disclaims all warranties regarding harmful effects, including curses and hexes, such disclaimer shall be binding unless it is unconscionably one-sided or results from fraud or duress. The burden of proving knowledge of a curse lies with the buyer seeking to void the deal; mere speculation about latent dangers does not suffice. Sellers must affirmatively warrant that they have reviewed the item for known defects before representation can be made as to its safety.

A blessing conferred by one vendor upon an article may serve as a factual predicate for implied warranty claims against subsequent transferees, if the blessing was intended to enhance value or reduce risk. However, a blessing alone does not displace express terms agreed upon between buyer and seller in later transactions. Each sale constitutes a separate contractual relationship with its own warranties and disclaimers independent of prior dealings.

The Desk shall have authority to investigate alleged breaches of warranty arising from undisclosed curses, including but not limited to inspection of the contested item, testimony from experts familiar with such enchantments, and examination of relevant records. Remedies available to aggrieved parties include rescission of the sale, refund of purchase price plus interest, compensation for consequential damages proximately caused by the curse, and equitable relief as appropriate under the circumstances.

Nothing herein shall be construed to limit or alter any rights afforded by existing common law doctrines of fraud, misrepresentation, breach of contract, or tortious interference with contractual relations insofar as they may apply independently to matters governed by this section. The provisions hereof are intended solely to codify and clarify prevailing standards relating to curses and warranties in commercial transactions involving magical artifacts.

body.heading: § 1101.3 Curse as Warranty Disclaimer; Blessing of Competing Vendor — Continued — Continued
body.text:
The burden of disclosure extends beyond mere knowledge of a curse's presence to encompass the seller's duty to warn against its potential activation or escalation. Failure to provide such notice, where reasonably foreseeable, may constitute a breach of implied warranty regardless of actual intent to defraud. Thus, a vendor who knows that their goods are cursed and sells them without warning assumes liability for any resulting harm, even if no direct magical contact occurs between buyer and seller.

Furthermore, a blessing conferred upon property by a party with a competing interest may be deemed voidable at the option of the original owner. For example, if a debtor pledges cursed land to secure a loan and the lender subsequently blesses it in hopes of mitigating risk, such act does not extinguish the underlying defect. The blessing is merely a gesture of goodwill unless accompanied by explicit renunciation of prior claims or conditions attached thereto. Courts will scrutinize the motives behind any post-sale ritualistic enhancement to determine whether it was undertaken in good faith or as an attempt to obscure liability.

In cases involving multiple transactions of the same cursed item, each party remains liable for their own conduct independently of others' actions. A seller who knowingly transfers a cursed object cannot later disclaim responsibility merely because subsequent owners have also dealt with it improperly. The chain of title does not absolve anyone from their obligations under law unless expressly released by all interested parties in writing. This principle ensures that the original wrongdoer remains accountable for initiating the curse's propagation, even if others amplify its effects downstream.

Finally, remedies available against a cursed vendor include rescission of contract, damages for losses incurred, and injunctive relief to prevent further harm. Punitive sanctions may also apply where malice or gross negligence is proven beyond a reasonable doubt. The goal is not only compensation but deterrence—to discourage reckless handling of dangerous artifacts that threaten public safety. Only through strict enforcement can the Accords maintain order amidst these treacherous forces.

body.heading: § 1101.4 Implied Warranty of Non-Maleficence
body.text:
Whereas the foregoing sections address express warranties and disclaimers, this section establishes an implied covenant running with every magical transaction. By their very nature, enchanted items possess latent dangers unknown to the casual observer; hence, sellers are deemed to warrant that such risks have been fully disclosed prior to transfer of title. Failure to provide adequate warning renders any sale void ab initio, regardless of apparent consent or consideration paid. This principle finds its roots in the ancient maxim: "No spell unspoken, no harm unaverted."

The seller's duty extends beyond mere disclosure of known defects; they must actively investigate potential hazards inherent to the item's magic. For instance, a merchant selling a cursed dagger must ascertain whether it carries any malignant properties that could affect the buyer or their associates. Negligence in this regard constitutes breach of contract and grounds for rescission. Similarly, buyers are obligated to exercise due diligence in verifying claims made by sellers regarding an item's history and condition. Blind acceptance of assertions without corroboration shifts liability onto the purchaser should adverse consequences ensue.

In cases where both parties act in good faith but misunderstanding prevails, equitable remedies may apply rather than harsh penalties. A court might order restitution of purchase price plus reasonable expenses incurred during investigation or repair efforts. Alternatively, specific performance could compel delivery of a properly enchanted substitute if feasible without undue hardship. The ultimate goal remains restoration of injured rights to their pre-transaction state, wherever practically possible under the circumstances.

This implied warranty operates independently of any express agreement between parties and survives attempts to contract around it via fine print or oral stipulations. It reflects society's collective judgment that magical commerce demands heightened standards of care due to the extraordinary powers involved. Those who would engage in such trade must accept these obligations willingly, understanding that failure to comply invites serious repercussions. Only through mutual vigilance can the delicate balance of magic and law be preserved for generations to come.

see § 1001.8 Lead-to-Gold Reporting Threshold; see § 200.4 Suspension and Lapse; see § 300.5 Research Copies of Quiet Items

sections.title: Blessing of a Competing Vendor
sections.brief: A blessing sold against a rival is advertising, then fraud if it binds.

body.heading: Blessing of a Competing Vendor
body.text:
Under the jurisdiction of the Autumnwood Accords and the oversight of the Accords Desk, all magical services provided by licensed practitioners within the Midlands shall be subject to the standards of fair commerce and arcane integrity. While the Mages' Guild acknowledges the inherent right of a practitioner to solicit patronage, the application of liturgical or protective enchantments for the express purpose of undermining a specific, identified competitor is strictly regulated. A blessing, by its fundamental nature, is a metaphysical enhancement of a subject's state; however, when such a blessing is structured to actively diminish the efficacy, reputation, or commercial viability of a rival entity, it transcends the realm of standard mercantile competition and enters the sphere of regulated magical advertising.

Any practitioner who offers a "Blessing of Superiority" or a "Ward of Market Dominance" that specifically names, targets, or references a competing vendor shall be required to file a Notice of Commercial Intent with the Accords Desk prior to the casting of said enchantment. Such notices must clearly delineate the scope of the blessing to ensure it does not infringe upon the existing magical protections or established trade rights of the aforementioned rival. If a blessing is sold as a means to "outshine" a competitor without specific naming, it remains a permissible act of promotion, provided it does not utilize prohibited schools of magic as defined in § 1.6. However, the moment a practitioner employs a binding oath or a persistent enchantment that actively suppresses the rival's ability to conduct business—such as a "Curse of Diminished Appeal" or a "Ward of Consumer Aversion"—the act shall be reclassified as fraudulent conduct.

Fraud, as defined under § 1001.1, occurs when a magical effect is deployed with the intent to deceive the public or to create an artificial monopoly through coercive arcane means. A blessing that binds a customer to a specific vendor by magically inhibiting their ability to seek services from a competitor is a violation of the Accords. Such binding effects are considered predatory and shall be subject to immediate dissolution by the Aegis Magi. Practitioners found guilty of selling such binding blessings shall be liable for restitution to the affected vendor and may face sanctions under § 800.1. Furthermore, any practitioner who knowingly sells a blessing that contains hidden "leash" mechanics—where the blessing provides a benefit to the buyer while simultaneously siphoning mana or influence from a rival—shall be subject to the Paradox Trial for the use of deceptive and destabilizing magic.

The Distinction between legitimate promotion and prohibited fraud rests upon the presence of a "binding" element. If the magic merely encourages a preference, it is a matter of trade; if the magic removes the agency of the consumer or the viability of the rival through persistent, involuntary arcane interference, it is a breach of the Accords. Practitioners are encouraged to consult the Goodstyle Artisans for approved methods of non-binding promotional magic to ensure compliance with these statutes. Any dispute regarding the "competitive reach" of a blessing shall be mediated by Archmage Veyra’s office, though the burden of proof shall rest upon the petitioner to demonstrate that the blessing in question is non-consensual in its suppression of the rival's interests.

body.heading: § 1101.4 Blessing of a Competing Vendor
body.text:
A blessing offered by a vendor who is known to have a competing interest in the transaction shall be deemed suspicious and subject to immediate inquiry by the Desk. Under no circumstances may such a blessing be relied upon as valid consideration unless it has been fully disclosed and ratified in writing by all parties involved. Any attempt to conceal or misrepresent the nature of the conflict shall constitute grounds for disciplinary action up to and including revocation of licensure.

The provision is intended to prevent vendors from using their influence to artificially enhance the perceived value of goods they are selling, thereby defrauding buyers and undermining fair market practices. Vendors must disclose any personal or financial ties to competing entities before offering blessings that could materially affect the outcome of a deal. Failure to do so renders such blessings void ab initio and exposes the vendor to liability for damages incurred by aggrieved parties.

The Desk shall maintain a registry of all known conflicts of interest involving licensed vendors, making this information available upon request to any party engaged in transactions with said vendors. This transparency requirement is designed to empower consumers to make informed decisions regarding their purchases while holding vendors accountable for unethical conduct. Regular audits and investigations will be conducted to ensure compliance with these provisions and to identify any systemic issues requiring remedial action.

Blessings tainted by undisclosed conflicts of interest shall be treated as fraudulent misrepresentations under applicable law, giving rise to claims for rescission, restitution, and consequential damages. Vendors found guilty of violating this section may face additional penalties including fines, suspensions, and permanent expulsion from the Guild. The Desk retains broad discretion in determining appropriate sanctions based on the severity of the violation and its impact on market integrity.

Parties are strongly urged to seek independent legal counsel before entering into any transaction involving blessings from vendors with potential competing interests. Failure to do so does not excuse reliance on tainted blessings or limit liability for resulting losses. The burden remains on each party to exercise due diligence in protecting their own interests and avoiding conflicts that may compromise the fairness of a deal.

This section applies only to blessings offered within the context of commercial transactions between licensed vendors and consumers. Private arrangements unrelated to business activities are outside the scope of these regulations, though they may still be subject to general principles of contract law and ethical conduct expected of all Guild members. The Desk reserves the right to interpret this provision as necessary to preserve the integrity of the marketplace and protect public welfare from deceptive practices.

body.heading: § 1101.4 Blessing of a Competing Vendor — Continued
body.text:
A vendor's blessing is not merely an expression of goodwill but a binding magical contract that alters the legal status of goods. When a seller invokes their divine patron or ancestral spirits to sanctify merchandise, they create a metaphysical warranty that persists beyond the transaction. However, this blessing may be invoked against competitors who violate its terms, effectively weaponizing sacred oaths as trade barriers.

The law recognizes that such blessings often function as de facto monopolies when properly enforced. If a vendor's patron grants exclusive protection to their products, rival merchants cannot legally replicate these effects without committing ritual fraud under § 1001.4. The Accords further prohibit using blessed items in comparative advertising unless explicit disclaimers accompany all claims of superiority. Unsubstantiated assertions of magical dominance constitute false propaganda punishable by fines and temporary suspension of licensure.

Enforcement mechanisms include immediate seizure of offending goods upon complaint, followed by a full judicial review of blessing authenticity. In cases where rival vendors deliberately undermine another's sanctified wares through dark magic or sabotage, they face enhanced penalties for both economic harm and desecration of sacred bonds. The Guild maintains detailed registries of all blessings granted to licensed sellers, allowing rapid verification during disputes.

The underlying principle remains that commerce must never supersede spiritual obligations. When a merchant invokes divine forces to secure market advantage, they enter into a complex web of metaphysical liabilities. Failure to honor these sacred duties invites retribution not only from offended patrons but also from the Guild itself, which views such practices as inherently destabilizing to the broader magical economy. Thus, blessings wielded in commercial contexts are treated with the utmost seriousness, reflecting their profound impact on both tangible profits and intangible spiritual realities.

body.heading: § 1101.4 Blessing of a Competing Vendor — Advertising by Binding
body.text: A blessing sold on behalf of a vendor who stands in competition with the original seller shall be deemed, at law, to constitute an act of advertising for that competitor's benefit. See § 705.3 Prohibition Against Improper Solicitation; § 1204.5 Undue Influence by Third Parties. If such blessing further binds the purchaser—whether through a written contract or oral agreement—the original seller may bring suit for damages, including reasonable out-of-pocket expenses and lost profits directly traceable to the sale of the competing blessing. The burden rests on the complaining party to prove causation with particularity; mere speculation as to what the customer might have purchased from them instead is insufficient to establish standing under § 1204.6 Standing Requirements. Moreover, any clause within a blessing purporting to waive this right or limit damages shall be held void as contrary to public policy and good morals. See § 705.8 Unconscionable Provisions; § 1203.1 Waiver of Statutory Rights Invalidity. The Desk reserves the authority to issue a cease-and-desist order against any entity found engaging in such practices, and may refer matters for criminal prosecution where appropriate. This provision ensures that vendors retain full control over their commercial interests, even when third parties attempt to exploit binding arrangements for gain.

body.heading: § 1101.4 Blessing of a Competing Vendor — Advertising by Binding — Continued
body.text:
A vendor's blessing, when offered in direct competition with an established merchant, constitutes not merely an offer but an act of public advertising. The binding nature of the spell serves to guarantee the efficacy and value of the goods or services purchased through that blessing; thus, it functions as a form of promotional endorsement carried out via magical compulsion rather than mere words. This practice is permissible so long as it does not violate other provisions of the Accords, particularly those governing unfair competition and deceptive trade practices under Title 8.

However, when such a blessing explicitly targets a specific rival vendor's customer base or reputation, it crosses into the realm of malicious intent. In this context, the spell operates less as an advertisement and more as a weaponized tool to undermine a competitor's market position. The law views these acts with extreme skepticism, for they strike at the heart of fair commercial dealings. A blessing cast solely to degrade another business's standing may be deemed actionable under § 800.1(D) as intentional interference with economic relations.

Furthermore, if the binding clause within such a competitive blessing restricts the addressee from patronizing rival establishments or purchasing alternative products, it effectively creates an exclusive contractual obligation enforced by magic rather than consent. Such clauses are void ab initio under § 200.4(A)(1), as they constitute an impermissible restraint on trade. The Archmage's Court shall invalidate any offending enchantment and assess damages against the casting mage for tortious interference, alongside appropriate fines payable to the injured party.

The Desk advises all merchants to exercise great care in crafting blessings intended for commercial purposes. While promotion of one's own wares is lawful, targeting a competitor with binding magic invites severe repercussions under both civil and penal statutes. It is incumbent upon each vendor to consider the broader implications of their magical marketing strategies before committing them to parchment or spellbook. The Accords exist to protect all parties engaged in legitimate commerce from exploitation by rogue mages seeking personal gain at another's expense.

see § 800.1(D) Intentional Interference with Economic Relations; see § 200.4(A)(1) Impermissible Restraints on Trade; see § 900.5 False Provenance of Relics — Deceptive Marketing Practices under the guise of blessing may constitute fraud. A blessing that binds a customer exclusively to one vendor violates principles of free trade and fair competition outlined in Title 2. Such acts warrant swift legal intervention by the Archmage's Court to prevent further harm to innocent merchants. The Desk urges all practitioners to review their commercial enchantments carefully before deployment, ensuring they comply with both letter and spirit of these laws. Failure to do so may result in substantial penalties under applicable statutes.

body.heading: § 1101.4 Blessing of a Competing Vendor — Advertising by Binding; Fraudulent Res
body.text:
A vendor shall not offer a blessing that simultaneously binds the recipient to purchase exclusively from a competitor, as such an arrangement constitutes fraudulent restraint of trade under common law principles and violates § 1101.2 regarding unconscionable terms. Any contract clause mandating exclusive patronage of another entity in exchange for magical enhancement is void ab initio, regardless of its inclusion within the blessing's enchantments.

Furthermore, a vendor who employs binding magic to compel a customer into buying from them after receiving superior goods or services commits misrepresentation and unjust enrichment. The compelled purchase shall be subject to rescission upon proof that the transaction resulted solely from magical coercion rather than voluntary assent. This rule applies even if the initial blessing was legitimate and the subsequent restraint appears superficially consensual, as long as the totality of circumstances demonstrates undue influence.

The prohibition extends to subtle forms of binding such as charm, compulsion, or alteration of memory that impairs judgment regarding commercial decisions. A vendor who uses any such technique to secure a monopoly over their client's spending habits violates this section and faces disciplinary action under § 1100 et seq. The burden lies on the accuser to demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that magical interference materially affected the victim's ability to negotiate fair terms.

Exceptions exist where both parties knowingly enter into an exclusive arrangement for legitimate business reasons, such as trade secrets or specialized expertise. However, any clause requiring total submission of will to another party remains impermissible regardless of commercial justification. The Guild maintains a strict stance against magical coercion in economic contexts to preserve free market principles and individual autonomy.

Violations shall be prosecuted under the full weight of criminal statutes including extortion, fraud, and conspiracy where appropriate. Civil remedies include restitution, damages for emotional distress, and permanent injunctions barring future abusive practices. Repeat offenders risk revocation of all professional licenses and sanctions up to and including imprisonment. The Desk retains sole discretion to determine penalties based on severity of offense and mitigating factors present in each case.

see § 1101.3 regarding valuation after alteration; see § 700.2 for guidelines on simulating consent under duress; see § 900.4 identifying fees owed for binding services rendered against one's will. This provision reinforces the Guild's commitment to protecting citizens from predatory magical practitioners who abuse their powers for financial gain at others' expense.

"Magic must serve humanity, not enslave it." — Archmage Veyra, Autumnwood Accords Preamble

sections.title: Transit Stamps
sections.brief: Planar instability surcharge. Archie-related invoices are not a defense.

body.heading: Transit Stamps
body.text:
The Accords Desk hereby establishes the mandatory requirement for Transit Stamps upon any manifestation of translocation magic that crosses established jurisdictional boundaries between the Midlands and neighboring territories. Any mage, regardless of factional affiliation—be it Conservator or Innovator—who utilizes a portal, rift, or teleportation circle to move sentient beings, sentient goods, or significant arcane masses must secure a stamped authorization from the local Aegis Magi before the final weaving of the spell. Failure to produce a valid Transit Stamp at the point of emergence shall result in immediate seizure of the transit vessel or the magical focus used to initiate the movement. The surcharge for these stamps is calculated based on the volume of the displaced space and the inherent magical pressure of the destination.

Furthermore, the Accords Desk explicitly clarifies the liability regarding specific administrative exemptions. It is strictly understood that any invoice, receipt, or correspondence originating from the individual known as Archie Miser shall not constitute a valid defense against the assessment of a Planar Instability Surcharge. While the holder of a Provisional Guild Pass may enjoy certain diplomatic protections regarding the Iron Mandate, such protections do not extend to the fiscal obligations of transit. If a mage attempts to utilize an Archie-related invoice to offset the costs of a planar breach or a high-pressure translocation, the Accords Desk shall deem the invoice null and void for the purposes of this specific surcharge. Mages are encouraged to maintain separate ledgers for political navigation and logistical transit to avoid such clerical complications.

In instances where the destination of a transit is obscured by atmospheric interference or planar shifting, the mage is required to pay a "High-Risk" premium. This premium is levied to compensate the Guild for the potential degradation of the Midlands' ley lines caused by erratic arrivals. See § 1201.2 for rules regarding the evasion of such tolls. Any attempt to bypass the stamping process through the use of "natural" rifts or uncatalogued fissures is strictly prohibited; such actions are to be treated as unauthorized field use and may be subject to the Paradox Trial. Mages found in violation of these requirements may have their translocation foci temporarily bound by the Aegis Magi until all outstanding surcharges are settled in full.

body.heading: Planar Tolls
body.text:
The Accords Desk mandates that all planar tolls must be paid in full prior to the opening of any dimensional aperture. This requirement is designed to ensure that the Guild can maintain the integrity of the Midlands' magical infrastructure against the erosion caused by constant external peering and internal extraction. Mages who attempt to evade these tolls through the use of "Shadow-Leaping" or other clandestine methods of movement are in violation of the Accords. Such evasion is not merely a fiscal offense but a breach of the collective stability maintained by the Conservators. Any mage caught evading a toll shall be subject to immediate detention and a formal inquiry by the Aegis Magi.

Corridor courtesy is a primary tenet of the Accords regarding the use of shared magical conduits. When utilizing established "highways" of mana, mages are expected to maintain a steady flow and avoid "magical drafting," which is the act of riding the wake of another mage's translocation spell to save on personal mana expenditure or toll costs. Drafting is considered a form of theft and shall be prosecuted as such. Mages must maintain a respectful distance from one another during transit to prevent harmonic interference, which can lead to localized reality fractures or the unintended displacement of nearby flora and fauna.

Should a mage find a toll to be exorbitant or the corridor to be under-maintained, they are instructed to file a formal grievance with the Accords Desk rather than attempting to bypass the gate. The Guild does not recognize "self-service" toll reduction. Any mage who attempts to sabotage a toll gate or use a "blanking" spell to hide their transit signature from the Aegis Magi will be flagged for a Paradox Trial. The Guild’s primary objective is the preservation of the Midlands; therefore, the stability of the toll system is paramount. Mages are reminded that the Iron Mandate does not provide any sanctuary for those who violate the internal fiscal codes of the Autumnwood Accords.

body.heading: Extraterritorial Casting into a Diet Chamber
body.text:
The Accords Desk strictly prohibits the unauthorized casting of spells into any designated "Diet Chamber" located outside the primary jurisdiction of the Autumnwood Accords. A Diet Chamber is defined as any consecrated or sequestered space dedicated to the consumption of sustenance, ritualistic feeding, or the preservation of biological matter for consumption. Casting into such a space, particularly when the magic involves transmutation, necromancy, or the alteration of biological properties, is considered a severe violation of the sanctity of the Midlands' social order. Such actions are often associated with the illicit practices of the Silver Flame or the forbidden schools monitored by Archmage Theron.

Mages who believe they have a legitimate requirement to interact with a Diet Chamber—such as for the purpose of large-scale banquet enchantment or the preservation of perishable goods for a public festival—must not cast directly into the chamber. Instead, the mage shall be required to file a formal Letter of Intent with the local Aegis Magi at least forty-eight hours prior to the intended casting. This letter must detail the specific spells to be used, the expected duration of the enchantment, and the names of the primary casters. Once the letter is filed and approved, a temporary permit will be issued, allowing for the supervised execution of the magic.

Direct casting into a Diet Chamber without a filed letter will result in the immediate seizure of the mage's focus and a mandatory appearance before the Council of Peers for a Paradox Trial. The Guild takes these restrictions seriously to prevent the contamination of food supplies and the desecration of sacred feeding grounds. This rule applies regardless of whether the chamber is public or private. Mages are cautioned that "minor" charms intended to enhance flavor or temperature are still subject to these filing requirements if they involve the fundamental alteration of the food's essence. For questions regarding the specific wording of a Letter of Intent, mages may consult the archives of the Conservators.

body.heading: Cartography Sold as a License to Raid
body.text:
The Accords Desk hereby clarifies the legal distinction between the possession of a map and the authorization of a magical operation. It is a strictly enforced rule that any cartographic document, including those of the One-T mountain range or other high-altitude regions, is classified solely as a navigational aid. The mere possession of a map, regardless of its detail, provenance, or the inclusion of marked "points of interest," does not constitute a license to raid, mine, or perform any form of extractive magic in the depicted area. Mages who attempt to use a map as a "permit" to enter restricted zones or to conduct unauthorized field research shall be held liable for trespassing and unauthorized arcane interference.

Mages are reminded that the One-T mountain is a site of significant geological and magical sensitivity. The use of "One-T cartography" as a justification for entering the peaks without a specific Expedition Permit is a violation of the Accords. A map shows where a mage *can* go; it does not grant the right to *do* anything once they arrive. Any mage found in possession of a map who is subsequently caught engaging in unauthorized "raid" behavior—defined as the organized extraction of minerals, relics, or mana-rich flora—will be subject to immediate arrest by the Aegis Magi. The Guild will not recognize the "exploration" defense as a valid excuse for the violation of territorial boundaries.

Furthermore, the sale of maps by Goodstyle Artisans or other licensed merchants is encouraged, but these sales are not tied to any underlying rights of access.
